signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: What is internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: A disorder of horizontal conjugate gaze caused by a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). On gaze away from the lesion the ipsilateral eye fails to adduct while the contralateral abducting eye shows nystagmus. Convergence is typically preserved.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Which tract is lesioned in INO, and what does it connect?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), which connects the CN VI (abducens) nucleus in the pons to the CONTRALATERAL CN III (oculomotor / medial-rectus) subnucleus in the midbrain, coordinating horizontal conjugate gaze.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Describe the classic eye-movement findings of a RIGHT INO.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: On attempted LEFT gaze (away from the lesion) the RIGHT eye fails to adduct (cross the midline), and the LEFT (abducting) eye develops horizontal nystagmus. INO is named for the side of the adduction failure / MLF lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Which sign distinguishes INO from a medial-rectus / third-nerve palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: Convergence. In INO convergence is typically PRESERVED (the medial rectus and CN III are intact); in a medial-rectus / CN III palsy convergence also fails.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Which eye shows the nystagmus in INO?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: The contralateral, ABDUCTING eye (dissociated / abduction nystagmus). The ipsilateral adducting eye is the one that fails to move in.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: On which side of the lesion is adduction impaired in INO?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: The IPSILATERAL eye (the eye on the same side as the MLF lesion) fails to adduct, seen on gaze AWAY from the lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Bilateral INO in a YOUNG patient is which diagnosis until proven otherwise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: Multiple sclerosis (demyelination of both MLFs) — the classic exam sign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Unilateral INO in an OLDER / vasculopathic patient is most likely due to what?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: A brainstem (pontine) stroke — a small-vessel infarct of the MLF.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: What is the age/laterality fork for the cause of INO?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back:
• Bilateral INO in a young patient → multiple sclerosis
  • unilateral INO in an older patient → brainstem (pontine) stroke.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: List causes of INO other than MS and stroke.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back:
• Brainstem tumour / glioma
  • Wernicke's encephalopathy
  • SLE / vasculitis
  • infection and trauma.
Drug toxicity (phenytoin, lithium, tricyclics) is a rare cause — these far more often produce gaze-evoked nystagmus with ataxia than a true INO. Myasthenia can produce a pseudo-INO.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: What is one-and-a-half syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: An INO plus an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy, from a lesion of the MLF PLUS the abducens nucleus / PPRF on the same side. The only residual horizontal movement is abduction of the contralateral eye.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: What is WEBINO?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: 'Wall-eyed bilateral INO' — a bilateral INO with exotropia (the eyes are divergent at rest), from a midline MIDBRAIN lesion involving both MLFs AND the CN III medial-rectus subnuclei. It is that subnuclear involvement that makes the eyes diverge at rest.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Why is the adduction lag of INO often best seen on fast saccades?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: The adduction deficit can be subtle; rapid horizontal saccades exaggerate the slowing of the affected adducting eye, which lags behind the abducting eye.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: What symptoms does a patient with INO report?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: Often none — the eyes are aligned in primary gaze, so INO is frequently found on examination rather than complained of. When symptomatic: horizontal diplopia or blurring on lateral gaze, and/or oscillopsia from the abducting-eye nystagmus.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: What is the key investigation in INO?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: MRI brain — showing a demyelinating plaque or an infarct in the dorsal pons / midbrain along the MLF.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: If MS is suspected as the cause of INO, what investigations are added?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: MRI brain and cord with contrast, and lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands where imaging alone is not sufficient. Visual evoked potentials (VEPs) are a selective adjunct to show subclinical optic-nerve involvement when the picture is equivocal, not a routine part of the work-up. MS is never diagnosed on MRI alone.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: If stroke is suspected as the cause of INO, what is the work-up?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back:
• MRI (DWI) +/- angiography
  • vascular risk factor assessment
  • and entry onto the acute stroke pathway with secondary prevention.
Note a normal early DWI does NOT rule out a small brainstem infarct — false negatives are commoner in the posterior circulation, so treat on clinical grounds and repeat the scan if the picture fits.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: How is an INO due to an MS relapse managed?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: Exclude infection / pseudo-relapse, then treat with oral methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 5 days (IV methylprednisolone if oral fails, is not tolerated, or admission is needed) (NICE). Steroids hasten recovery from the relapse but do not change the long-term outcome. Refer into the disease-modifying therapy pathway, plus supportive care.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: What red-flag combination points to a top-of-basilar / basilar-territory stroke?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: Acute INO WITH other brainstem signs. A vertical-gaze palsy with drowsiness points to a top-of-basilar (rostral midbrain / thalamic) stroke; quadriparesis with preserved awareness points to a ventral pontine 'locked-in' picture from basilar trunk occlusion. Either warrants urgent imaging.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: What is pseudo-INO and how is it distinguished?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: Myasthenia gravis can mimic INO exactly. It is fatigable and variable with a NORMAL pupil; test for fatigability and check anti-AChR antibodies with repetitive nerve stimulation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Which three bedside tests confirm and characterise an INO?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back:
• Test horizontal saccades and smooth pursuit (adduction lag)
  • look for the abducting-eye nystagmus
  • and test convergence (preserved in INO).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Why does convergence remain intact in INO?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: Convergence uses a separate supranuclear pathway to the CN III medial-rectus subnuclei that bypasses the MLF, so the intact medial rectus can still adduct on convergence despite failing on conjugate lateral gaze.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Onset of a demyelinating INO vs a vascular INO — how do they differ?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: A vascular (stroke) INO is typically abrupt in onset, whereas a demyelinating (MS) INO is more often subacute.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: Where anatomically does the MLF lesion lie in INO?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: In the dorsal (paramedian) pons / midbrain tegmentum, between the abducens nucleus (pons) and the contralateral oculomotor nucleus (midbrain).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: INO with ataxia and confusion in an alcoholic or malnourished patient — diagnosis and action?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: Wernicke's encephalopathy — give high-dose PARENTERAL (IV/IM) thiamine immediately, before or with any glucose; do not wait for confirmation. Oral thiamine is not adequate. Note the usual eye signs of Wernicke's are nystagmus and abduction weakness; INO is the less common one.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.front: What full examination should accompany the assessment of an INO?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.back: A full neurological exam looking for MS features (other CNS signs, previous episodes, optic neuritis) or stroke features and vascular risk factors, plus the other brainstem signs that flag a basilar-territory stroke.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: What is the first step in assessing any headache?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back:
Screen for red flags of a secondary (dangerous) cause before pattern-matching a primary headache. Key axes:
  • onset (thunderclap vs gradual)
  • time course
  • associated features
  • and age.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: List the key red flags in a headache history.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back:
• Thunderclap onset
  • fever + neck stiffness / photophobia
  • new headache >50 with scalp tenderness / jaw claudication
  • progressive headache worse on waking / coughing / lying with vomiting, focal signs or papilloedema
  • reduced GCS
  • immunosuppression / cancer
  • pregnancy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: A patient describes a sudden 'worst-ever' headache peaking within seconds. What must be excluded and how?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Subarachnoid haemorrhage — a thunderclap headache. Do an urgent CT head; if negative and SAH still suspected, lumbar puncture (≥12 h after onset) for xanthochromia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: A headache with fever, neck stiffness and photophobia suggests what?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Meningitis / encephalitis — give empirical antibiotics without delay (community: IM benzylpenicillin; hospital: IV ceftriaxone / cefotaxime, add amoxicillin for Listeria if >50 / immunocompromised), plus dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis and aciclovir if encephalitis; LP after CT if focal signs / reduced GCS.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: What are the features of giant cell arteritis and why is it an emergency?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: New headache >50 with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication and a tender / pulseless temporal artery, with a raised ESR / CRP. It threatens irreversible visual loss — give high-dose steroids immediately (before biopsy).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: Which headache features suggest raised intracranial pressure / a space-occupying lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Progressive headache, worse on waking, lying flat, coughing or straining (Valsalva), with vomiting, papilloedema, focal neurology, seizures or personality change.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: Which clues point to cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as the cause of headache?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Headache with seizures, focal deficits or raised ICP, especially in a prothrombotic state (pregnancy / puerperium, combined pill, thrombophilia, dehydration); confirm with CT / MR venography.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: What is idiopathic intracranial hypertension and who gets it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Raised ICP with no mass lesion — headache, papilloedema and transient visual obscurations, classically a young obese woman (± certain drugs). Risk to vision; managed with weight loss, acetazolamide ± shunt.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: What are the diagnostic features of migraine?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Episodic, often unilateral, throbbing headache lasting 4–72 h, moderate–severe, worse with activity, with nausea and photophobia / phonophobia (± aura).

A reversible focal neurological symptom preceding / accompanying the headache — classically visual (zig-zag lines, scotoma) spreading over 5–60 min then resolving; may be sensory or dysphasic. Migraine with aura contraindicates the combined oral contraceptive pill (ischaemic-stroke risk).

• Acute: a triptan + NSAID / paracetamol (± antiemetic)
  • Prophylaxis (if frequent / disabling): propranolol, amitriptyline or topiramate (avoid topiramate / valproate in pregnancy).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: What are the features of a tension-type headache?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Bilateral, band-like, pressing / tight pain of mild–moderate intensity, not aggravated by activity and without nausea. Managed with reassurance and simple analgesia.

A chronic daily headache caused by regular overuse of acute headache medication (≥15 days/month for simple analgesics, or ≥10 days/month for triptans, opioids or combination analgesics). Treated by withdrawing the overused medication.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: What are the features of cluster headache?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Severe unilateral orbital / temporal pain lasting 15–180 min, in bouts (often nocturnal / circadian), with ipsilateral autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, ptosis / miosis) and a restless, agitated patient.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: How is an acute cluster headache treated?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: High-flow 100% oxygen and subcutaneous (or nasal) sumatriptan. Prophylaxis is with verapamil.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: What is trigeminal neuralgia and how is it treated?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Paroxysmal, electric-shock-like facial pain in a trigeminal division, provoked by trigger zones (touch, chewing, cold). First-line treatment is carbamazepine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: How should you assess a headache in a pregnant woman?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: Always check the blood pressure and urine for protein to exclude pre-eclampsia / eclampsia (a red flag in pregnancy); also consider cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, which is commoner in pregnancy and the puerperium.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.front: When should carbon monoxide poisoning be suspected as a cause of headache?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.back: When several household members are affected, symptoms are worse at home / in winter and improve away from home; confirm with a carboxyhaemoglobin level and treat with high-flow oxygen.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: How should you classify a complaint of 'dizziness'?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back:
Into
  • vertigo (illusion of movement / spinning → vestibular)
  • presyncope (light-headed, near-faint → cardiovascular)
  • disequilibrium (unsteadiness on walking → cerebellar / sensory / drugs)
  • and psychogenic dizziness.

An illusion of movement (usually spinning) of the patient or their surroundings — a vestibular symptom, which is then divided into peripheral (labyrinth / vestibular nerve) and central (brainstem / cerebellum).

• Peripheral: abnormal head impulse test, unidirectional horizontal nystagmus, normal gait, often hearing symptoms
  • Central: normal head impulse, vertical / direction-changing nystagmus, severe gait ataxia and other brainstem / cerebellar signs.

A three-part bedside test in acute vestibular syndrome: Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew. It distinguishes peripheral from central causes and is more sensitive than early MRI for posterior circulation stroke.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: How is the head impulse test interpreted in acute vertigo?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back:
• An abnormal head impulse (a corrective catch-up saccade) is reassuring — peripheral
  • A NORMAL head impulse in a patient with acute continuous vertigo is worrying — central (stroke).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: What are the features and treatment of BPPV?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back: Brief (<1 min) positional vertigo triggered by head movement (turning in bed, looking up); diagnosed with the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre and treated with the Epley repositioning manoeuvre. Vestibular sedatives do not help in BPPV.

Both cause acute, prolonged (days) severe vertigo, often post-viral.
  • Vestibular neuritis has no hearing loss
  • labyrinthitis is the same picture plus hearing loss / tinnitus.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: What is the classic triad of Ménière's disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back: Episodic vertigo (20 min–hours) with fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and a sense of aural fullness. Managed with salt restriction, betahistine and diuretics.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: What features suggest an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back: Gradual unilateral sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus, sometimes with imbalance and (later) facial / trigeminal signs — a cerebellopontine-angle lesion; investigate with MRI of the internal acoustic meatus.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: Which features of acute vertigo point to a posterior circulation stroke?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back: A normal head impulse test, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, a skew deviation, other brainstem / cerebellar signs or inability to stand / walk unaided — the central 'INFARCT' pattern on HINTS.
Recurrent vertigo accompanied by migrainous features (headache, photophobia, aura, or a migraine history) — a common central cause of episodic vertigo.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: What are the main causes of presyncope ('nearly fainting') dizziness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back: Cardiovascular — arrhythmia / heart block and orthostatic hypotension — plus anaemia and hypoglycaemia. It is light-headedness, not an illusion of movement.
A fall in BP on standing (≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic) causing light-headedness — from drugs, dehydration or autonomic failure; confirmed with lying-standing blood pressure.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: Why is dizziness in the elderly often described as disequilibrium?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back: Because it is frequently multifactorial — combined visual, proprioceptive, vestibular and cerebellar decline plus polypharmacy — producing unsteadiness on walking and a significant falls risk.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: How does nystagmus differ between peripheral and central vertigo?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back:
• Peripheral: unidirectional, horizontal (± torsional), suppressed by fixation (and fatigable on positional / Dix-Hallpike testing in BPPV)
  • Central: vertical, or direction-changing (changes with gaze direction), not suppressed by fixation.

Supportive — a short course (a few days) of a vestibular sedative / antiemetic (e.g. prochlorperazine) for the acute phase, then vestibular rehabilitation exercises to promote central compensation. Steroids are sometimes used but remain controversial.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.front: Why should vestibular sedatives (e.g. prochlorperazine) be used only short-term?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.back: They help acute severe peripheral vertigo but impair central compensation if continued, prolonging symptoms — so use them only for a few days and not in BPPV or chronic dizziness.

• Acute attacks: vestibular sedatives / antiemetics
  • Prevention: salt restriction, betahistine and sometimes diuretics; refer to ENT for troublesome disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What is the first step when a patient reports 'weakness'?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: Confirm it is true loss of power (not fatigue, pain-limited movement or apparent weakness), then localise the lesion — UMN, LMN, neuromuscular junction or muscle — and note the distribution.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What are the signs of an upper motor neuron (UMN) lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back:
• Increased tone / spasticity
  • hyperreflexia
  • upgoing plantars (Babinski)
  • clonus
  • no wasting (± disuse)
  • and a pyramidal pattern of weakness (weak arm extensors, weak leg flexors).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What are the signs of a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back:
• Reduced tone
  • muscle wasting
  • fasciculations
  • hyporeflexia / areflexia
  • and downgoing or absent plantars.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What is the hallmark of neuromuscular junction (NMJ) weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: Fatigable weakness (worse with use / later in the day) with normal reflexes, tone and sensation — e.g. myasthenia gravis (ptosis, diplopia, bulbar).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What is the typical pattern of a myopathy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: Proximal, symmetrical weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, combing hair) with normal reflexes (until late) and no sensory loss; the CK is often raised.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: How does the distribution of weakness help localise the lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back:
• Hemiparesis → contralateral brain
  • paraparesis → spinal cord
  • quadriparesis → high cord / brainstem / GBS / NMJ
  • proximal symmetrical → muscle
  • distal symmetrical → peripheral nerve.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What does an acute hemiparesis (unilateral face/arm/leg weakness) suggest?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: A stroke (contralateral cerebral lesion, usually UMN) — activate the stroke pathway (FAST, urgent CT, thrombolysis / thrombectomy window).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What does a spastic paraparesis with a sensory level indicate?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: A spinal cord lesion — e.g. compression, transverse myelitis or MS. With bladder / bowel involvement it is a neurosurgical emergency needing urgent MRI.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What is characteristic of motor neurone disease on examination?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: Mixed UMN and LMN signs (e.g. brisk reflexes with wasting and fasciculations) with no sensory loss and no sphincter involvement.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What are the features and key monitoring in Guillain-Barré syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: Ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia, often post-infective. Monitor the forced vital capacity (FVC) for respiratory failure — oxygen saturations fall late.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What are the features of myasthenia gravis and its key antibody?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: Fatigable weakness with ptosis, diplopia and bulbar symptoms, worse through the day; associated with anti-acetylcholine-receptor (anti-AChR) antibodies (or anti-MuSK) and thymic disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: How does Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome differ from myasthenia gravis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: Weakness that improves with use / repeated effort (opposite to MG), with reduced reflexes that return after exercise; it is paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer, anti-VGCC antibodies).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What are the main causes of a proximal myopathy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back:
• Inflammatory (poly / dermatomyositis)
  • endocrine (thyroid disease, Cushing's / steroids)
  • drugs (statins)
  • inherited dystrophies (Duchenne / Becker)
  • and metabolic causes.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: How do radiculopathy and peripheral neuropathy differ in pattern?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back:
• Radiculopathy: weakness in a myotome with dermatomal sensory loss and radicular pain (a single root)
  • Peripheral neuropathy: distal, symmetrical 'glove & stocking' weakness / sensory loss.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: What is the pyramidal pattern of weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: In a UMN lesion, the upper-limb extensors and lower-limb flexors are preferentially weak (flexors stronger in the arm, extensors stronger in the leg).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: How are the investigations for weakness guided by localisation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back:
• UMN → CT / MRI brain or MRI spine
  • LMN / NMJ / muscle → nerve conduction studies / EMG, CK, TFTs, anti-AChR, and LP for GBS.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: Why monitor FVC rather than oxygen saturations in acute neuromuscular weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back: In GBS or myasthenic crisis, ventilatory failure develops from respiratory-muscle weakness; a falling FVC detects this early, whereas oxygen saturations drop late (a pre-terminal sign).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.front: How do the signs of cord compression and cauda equina syndrome differ?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.back:
• Cord compression: UMN legs (spastic, hyperreflexic), a sensory level and bladder / bowel dysfunction
  • Cauda equina: LMN legs (flaccid, areflexic), saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention ± back / radicular pain.
Both need emergency MRI.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: As numbness / loss, paraesthesia (tingling / pins and needles) or dysaesthesia (unpleasant or painful abnormal sensation) — then localise by the pattern of loss and the modalities affected.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: Which modalities travel in the dorsal columns, and how do they decussate?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Fine touch, vibration and proprioception (joint-position sense). They ascend ipsilaterally and decussate in the medulla.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: Which modalities travel in the spinothalamic tract, and where do they cross?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Pain and temperature (and crude touch). Fibres decussate within 1–2 segments of entering the cord, then ascend contralaterally.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: What is dissociated sensory loss and what does it localise to?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Loss of one modality set with preservation of the other (e.g. lost pain / temperature but intact vibration / proprioception). It localises the lesion to the spinal cord.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: What is the sensory pattern of a mononeuropathy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Sensory loss confined to one peripheral nerve’s territory (e.g. median nerve in carpal tunnel) — often with weakness in that nerve’s muscles.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: What is the pattern and differential of a polyneuropathy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back:
Distal, symmetrical ‘glove and stocking’ loss (length-dependent). Causes:
  • diabetes
  • alcohol
  • B12 deficiency
  • drugs
  • chronic kidney disease
  • and hereditary (Charcot-Marie-Tooth).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: What is the sensory pattern of a radiculopathy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Dermatomal sensory loss with radicular (shooting) pain and often myotomal weakness — from a single nerve-root lesion (e.g. disc prolapse).
A spinal cord lesion — sensory loss below a horizontal level on the trunk. Causes include cord compression, transverse myelitis and MS; with weakness / bladder involvement it is an emergency.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: Describe the sensory findings in Brown-Séquard (hemicord) syndrome.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Ipsilateral loss of vibration / proprioception (dorsal column) and ipsilateral UMN weakness, with contralateral loss of pain / temperature (spinothalamic) below the lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: What is the classic sensory pattern of syringomyelia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: A ‘cape’ distribution of dissociated loss — lost pain and temperature over the shoulders / arms with preserved dorsal columns (a central-cord lesion affecting decussating spinothalamic fibres).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: What are the sensory and motor features of subacute combined degeneration (B12)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Dorsal-column loss (vibration / proprioception, sensory ataxia, positive Romberg) with corticospinal signs — upgoing plantars but absent ankle jerks. Caused by B12 deficiency.
Infarction in the anterior spinal artery territory: loss of pain / temperature and motor function below the lesion, with dorsal columns (vibration / proprioception) spared.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: What sensory pattern suggests a brainstem lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Crossed sensory loss — ipsilateral face (trigeminal) and contralateral body — e.g. the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: What sensory pattern results from a thalamic lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Contralateral hemisensory loss of all modalities, sometimes followed by thalamic pain (Déjerine-Roussy syndrome).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: What are the features of cortical (parietal) sensory loss?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Primary modalities relatively preserved but higher sensory processing lost: impaired two-point discrimination, stereognosis, graphaesthesia and sensory inattention (extinction) on the contralateral side.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: Which sensory presentations are red flags needing urgent action?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back:
• A sensory level with leg weakness / bladder dysfunction (cord compression)
  • saddle anaesthesia with retention (cauda equina)
  • acute hemisensory loss (stroke)
  • and rapidly ascending sensory / motor loss (GBS).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: How are the investigations for sensory disturbance guided by localisation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back:
• Peripheral → nerve conduction studies, glucose / HbA1c, B12, TFTs, U&E
  • Root / cord → MRI spine
  • Central / hemisensory → MRI brain.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.front: How does carpal tunnel syndrome present, and how is it confirmed?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.back: Median-nerve paraesthesia / numbness (thumb, index, middle, radial half of ring finger), worse at night. Tinel’s and Phalen’s tests provoke it; confirmed with nerve conduction studies.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: How is tremor classified, and why does it matter?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back:
By activation:
  • rest tremor (present at rest, eased by movement) = Parkinsonism
  • postural tremor (arms outstretched) = essential / physiological
  • intention tremor (worse toward a target) = cerebellar.
This split drives the differential.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: What are the features of a Parkinsonian rest tremor?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back: A slow (4–6 Hz), asymmetric, ‘pill-rolling’ tremor present at rest and reduced by movement, with bradykinesia and rigidity.
Essential tremor and enhanced physiological tremor (anxiety, caffeine, thyrotoxicosis, drugs such as salbutamol / lithium, hypoglycaemia).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: What is an intention tremor and what does it localise to?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back: A tremor that worsens as the finger approaches a target (finger-nose test), with past-pointing / dysmetria — it localises to the cerebellum (or its connections).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: What are the features of essential tremor?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back: A bilateral, symmetric postural / action tremor that improves with alcohol, often with a family history (autosomal dominant); affects hands, head (titubation) and voice.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: What is enhanced physiological tremor and what exaggerates it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back:
A fine, fast postural tremor — the normal physiological tremor made worse by
  • anxiety
  • caffeine
  • thyrotoxicosis
  • drugs (salbutamol, lithium, valproate)
  • and hypoglycaemia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: How does drug-induced parkinsonism differ from Parkinson's disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back: It tends to be more symmetric and follows dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine); it usually improves on stopping the drug, unlike idiopathic Parkinson’s (which is asymmetric).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: What is the tremor of Wilson's disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back: A coarse proximal ‘wing-beating’ tremor in a young patient, with other neuro / psychiatric / liver features and Kayser-Fleischer rings; screen with caeruloplasmin (low) and copper studies.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: Which tremor is associated with thyrotoxicosis, and what else would you find?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back: A fine, fast postural tremor (enhanced physiological), with weight loss, heat intolerance, sweating, tachycardia / AF and a goitre; confirm with TFTs.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: Which drugs commonly cause or worsen tremor?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back:
• Beta-agonists (salbutamol)
  • lithium
  • sodium valproate
  • caffeine
  • and (as parkinsonism) dopamine antagonists (antipsychotics, metoclopramide).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: What are the features of lithium toxicity relevant to tremor?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back: A coarse tremor (a fine tremor is normal at therapeutic levels) with confusion, nausea / vomiting / diarrhoea, ataxia and seizures — check the lithium level and renal function.
A coarse tremor 6–12 h after the last drink can herald delirium tremens (agitation, hallucinations, autonomic instability, seizures) — a medical emergency; treat with benzodiazepines.
It is variable and distractible — it changes or stops when attention is diverted, and shows entrainment to a tapping rhythm; often abrupt onset.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: How do you distinguish essential tremor from Parkinson's disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back:
• Essential: symmetric, postural / action, improves with alcohol, family history, no bradykinesia
  • Parkinson’s: asymmetric, rest tremor, with bradykinesia and rigidity.
It is largely clinical: TFTs, caeruloplasmin (if young), glucose, drug / lithium review. A DaTscan separates Parkinsonian from essential tremor when unclear; MRI for cerebellar signs.
Propranolol (first-line; avoid in asthma / COPD — use primidone instead); alcohol gives short-term relief but is not a treatment. Deep brain stimulation for severe refractory cases.
A head (or trunk) tremor — a rhythmic nodding / bobbing — seen in essential tremor and in cerebellar disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.front: How does head involvement differ between Parkinson's disease and essential tremor?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.back:
• Essential tremor commonly causes a head tremor (titubation) and voice tremor
  • Parkinson’s disease typically spares the head / neck (its rest tremor affects the limbs, jaw and chin).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: What is ataxia, and what is the first step in assessing it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back: Incoordination out of proportion to weakness. The first step is to localise: cerebellar vs sensory (loss of proprioception) vs vestibular.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: How does Romberg's test distinguish the types of ataxia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back: Positive (steady with eyes open, falls when they close) = sensory ataxia. A cerebellar patient is unsteady with the eyes open or shut, so Romberg is negative — a classic exam trap.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: How do cerebellar hemisphere and vermis (midline) lesions differ?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back:
• A hemisphere lesion causes ipsilateral limb ataxia
  • a vermis / midline lesion (classically alcohol) causes truncal and gait ataxia while the limbs can look near-normal.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: On which side are cerebellar signs relative to the lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back: Ipsilateral — a right cerebellar-hemisphere lesion causes right-sided limb ataxia (unlike the contralateral signs of a cerebral lesion).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: What are the common causes of cerebellar ataxia?
What are the features of sensory ataxia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back:
Loss of joint-position and vibration sense (dorsal columns / peripheral nerve):
  • a positive Romberg
  • a high-stepping / stamping gait that is much worse in the dark
  • and pseudoathetosis.
Subacute combined degeneration of the cord: dorsal-column loss (sensory ataxia, positive Romberg) plus pyramidal signs — classically absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars; check serum B12.
A late (tertiary) manifestation of syphilis affecting the dorsal columns — sensory ataxia with lightning pains, areflexia and Argyll Robertson pupils.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: Why is acute ataxia treated as a stroke?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back: Sudden ataxia with headache / vomiting may be a cerebellar stroke — in the posterior fossa this risks brainstem compression and obstructive hydrocephalus, so it needs urgent imaging and neurosurgical review.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: What is the triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy and its key management point?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back: Ataxia + confusion + ophthalmoplegia / nystagmus. Give IV thiamine before any glucose, because a glucose load can precipitate or worsen it.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: What are the features of Friedreich's ataxia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back: A young patient with progressive ataxia; absent reflexes with extensor plantars, pes cavus, scoliosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and diabetes — autosomal recessive (FXN trinucleotide repeat).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: Which anticonvulsant classically causes ataxia in toxicity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back: Phenytoin — toxicity causes ataxia with nystagmus, slurred speech and drowsiness; check the phenytoin level.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: How does chronic alcohol misuse cause ataxia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back: It degenerates the cerebellar vermis, producing a predominantly truncal / gait ataxia; the limbs and finger-nose test are relatively spared.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: What are the features of vestibular ataxia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back: A gait that veers or falls toward one side with vertigo and nystagmus, but no limb ataxia or dysmetria — the problem is balance, not coordination.

• MRI brain (posterior fossa) for cerebellar signs
  • B12, glucose / HbA1c, TFTs and a phenytoin level
  • consider a paraneoplastic screen and genetic testing.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: How does the gait differ between cerebellar and sensory ataxia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back:
• Cerebellar: a wide-based, unsteady gait, poor heel-to-toe, unchanged by vision
  • Sensory: a high-stepping, stamping gait that is markedly worse in the dark or with eyes shut.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.front: Which systemic conditions cause cerebellar ataxia, and which are reversible?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ataxia.back:
• Potentially reversible: hypothyroidism, coeliac / gluten ataxia, phenytoin toxicity and thiamine deficiency
  • Paraneoplastic degeneration (e.g. anti-Yo) is usually irreversible and should prompt a malignancy search.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: What are the core diagnostic features of delirium?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back: An acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness, with a change in cognition — and it is reversible. Inattention is the hallmark.
Delirium: acute onset, fluctuating, inattention, clouded consciousness, reversible. Dementia: chronic, progressive, clear consciousness, memory-led. Delirium is often superimposed on dementia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: What are the three motor subtypes of delirium?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back:
• Hyperactive (agitated, hallucinating)
  • hypoactive (drowsy, withdrawn)
  • and mixed
The hypoactive type is easily missed and has the worst prognosis.
The 4AT and the CAM (Confusion Assessment Method); both test for acute onset / fluctuation and inattention (e.g. reciting the months of the year backwards).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: What must be checked first in every acutely confused patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back: The capillary glucose (hypoglycaemia is instantly treatable) and the oxygen saturations — then temperature and a search for infection.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: What does the PINCH ME mnemonic cover in delirium?

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back:
• Anticholinergics (oxybutynin, amitriptyline, antihistamines)
  • opioids
  • benzodiazepines
  • and steroids
withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines also causes it.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: What is included in a 'confusion screen'?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back: FBC, U&E, glucose, calcium, LFTs, TFTs, CRP; urine culture, blood cultures, CXR and ECG — to find an infective, metabolic or drug cause. (A urine dipstick is unreliable over 65 — diagnose UTI on the clinical picture, not the dip.)

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: When should a CT head be requested in a confused patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back: If there are focal neurological signs, a head injury or fall, anticoagulation, reduced / falling GCS, or no cause found on the confusion screen — to exclude a bleed (e.g. subdural).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: What is delirium tremens and how is it treated?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back: Severe alcohol withdrawal at ~48–72 h: agitation, hallucinations, tremor, autonomic instability and seizures. Treat with benzodiazepines (e.g. chlordiazepoxide) plus thiamine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: Why give thiamine before glucose in a malnourished confused patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back: To prevent precipitating or worsening Wernicke’s encephalopathy (ataxia, confusion, ophthalmoplegia) — a glucose load can deplete already-low thiamine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: What are the first-line management principles for delirium?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back:
Treat the underlying cause and use non-pharmacological measures first:
  • reorientation
  • familiar faces
  • sleep hygiene
  • hydration
  • glasses / hearing aids
  • and early mobilisation

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: When and how are antipsychotics used in delirium, and what is the key caution?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back: Only for severe distress or risk: short-term, low-dose haloperidol. Avoid antipsychotics in Parkinson’s disease and Lewy body dementia (neuroleptic sensitivity) — use lorazepam instead.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: Which easily reversible precipitants are classic in the confused elderly patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back: Urinary retention, constipation and infection (especially UTI and chest) — simple to find and to reverse.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.front: What is post-operative delirium and who is at risk?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Confusion / Deliriu.back: An acute confusion after surgery — very common in the elderly, driven by anaesthesia, pain / opioids, infection, dehydration and immobility; largely preventable.
In pseudodementia the patient has low mood, poor effort and gives “don’t know” answers, with a relatively acute onset; cognition improves when the depression is treated.
In psychosis the level of consciousness is clear and delusions are fixed and systematised; delirium has a clouded, fluctuating consciousness with inattention.
It is associated with increased mortality, longer hospital stays, higher rates of institutionalisation and a raised risk of subsequent dementia — it is never ‘just confusion’.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: What two components are needed for consciousness, and where do they arise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Arousal (the brainstem reticular activating system) and awareness (the cortex). Coma follows a brainstem lesion or widespread cortical dysfunction.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: How is the Glasgow Coma Scale scored?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Best Eye opening /4, Verbal response /5 and Motor response /6, summed out of 15 (minimum 3). Always record the trend and the components, not just the total.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: At what GCS is the airway considered unsafe, and what is the action?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: GCS ≤ 8 — the patient cannot protect their airway; get anaesthetic / critical-care help to intubate.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: What are the immediately reversible causes to treat in every comatose patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Glucose (hypoglycaemia — ‘Don’t Ever Forget Glucose’), naloxone (opioids) and thiamine (Wernicke’s / malnutrition); correct hypoxia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: How do the pupils help separate structural from metabolic coma?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Most metabolic / toxic comas preserve the pupillary light reflex (opioids are the pinpoint-but-reactive exception). Asymmetrical or fixed pupils suggest a structural lesion needing urgent CT.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: What features suggest a structural cause of coma?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Focal / asymmetrical neurology, unequal or fixed pupils, lateralising weakness and a sudden onset — e.g. a bleed, infarct or mass.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: What features suggest a metabolic or toxic cause of coma?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Symmetrical signs, reactive pupils even when deep, a fluctuating level, and myoclonus or asterixis; onset is usually more gradual.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: What are the signs of raised intracranial pressure with impending coning?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: A falling GCS with a fixed, dilated pupil (third-nerve / uncal herniation) and the Cushing response — hypertension with bradycardia ± irregular breathing.

• Secure the airway
  • head-up 30°
  • osmotic therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline)
  • maintain oxygenation / BP
  • urgent CT head
  • and call neurosurgery

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: What toxidrome causes coma with pinpoint pupils and a low respiratory rate?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Opioid toxicity — pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression; reverse with naloxone.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: What breathing pattern and breath suggest DKA as a cause of reduced consciousness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Deep, sighing Kussmaul breathing with a ketotic (fruity) breath and high glucose — diabetic ketoacidosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: Why give thiamine before glucose in a malnourished comatose patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: A glucose load can precipitate or worsen Wernicke’s encephalopathy in a thiamine-deplete patient — give thiamine first (or together).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: Which brainstem reflexes are tested in the assessment of coma?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Pupillary light, corneal, gag / cough and oculocephalic (doll’s eyes) reflexes — they localise the level of brainstem involvement.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: What is non-convulsive status epilepticus and how is it confirmed?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Ongoing seizure activity without prominent convulsions — a fluctuating reduced consciousness with subtle twitching or eye deviation; confirmed on EEG.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: What blood tests form the core coma work-up?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Glucose, U&E, LFTs, calcium, ABG, FBC / CRP, toxicology (paracetamol / salicylate) and ammonia; blood cultures if septic.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: When is a lumbar puncture performed in a comatose patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: When meningitis or encephalitis is suspected — but only after a CT head if there are focal signs or features of raised ICP.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: In suspected meningitis or encephalitis, why must treatment not wait for the CT/LP?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.back: Give empirical treatment immediately — IV ceftriaxone (± amoxicillin for Listeria in the elderly) and aciclovir if encephalitis is possible — because any delay increases mortality; do not wait for imaging or the LP result.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Consciousne.front: Besides drugs, name common metabolic causes of coma.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: What is a seizure, and what is the first step in describing one?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: A paroxysm of abnormal, synchronous cortical electrical activity. First classify it as focal (one region) or generalised (both hemispheres from onset).
By awareness: focal aware (consciousness retained) vs focal impaired-awareness; either may spread to a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure. Note motor signs, automatisms and aura.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: What are the main types of generalised seizure?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: Tonic-clonic, absence, myoclonic, tonic and atonic — all involve both hemispheres from the outset with loss of awareness.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: What features suggest a temporal lobe (focal) seizure?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: An aura — déjà-vu, a rising epigastric sensation, odd smells — followed by impaired awareness with automatisms (lip-smacking, fumbling).
A seizure lasting ≥ 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness between them — a medical emergency.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: Outline the emergency management of status epilepticus.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back:
• ABC, high-flow O2, check glucose
  • IV lorazepam (buccal midazolam / PR diazepam if no access), repeat once at 10 min
  • then IV levetiracetam / phenytoin / valproate
  • refractory → RSI & anaesthesia

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: A woman has a seizure in late pregnancy or postpartum. What is the diagnosis and treatment until proven otherwise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: Eclampsia — treat with magnesium sulfate (and control blood pressure); it is the assumed cause of a peripartum seizure.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: How do you distinguish an epileptic seizure from syncope?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: Epileptic: lateral tongue-bite, prolonged post-ictal confusion, cyanosis. Syncope: an upright trigger, pre-syncopal warning and rapid recovery (brief myoclonic jerks can still occur).

• Eyes closed and resisted
  • waxing-waning or asynchronous movements
  • pelvic thrusting
  • gradual onset
  • long duration
  • and no true post-ictal state or acidosis

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: Why does a new focal seizure in an adult need urgent imaging?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: It is a structural lesion (brain tumour, vascular lesion or old scar) until an MRI proves otherwise.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: Which metabolic and toxic factors provoke seizures?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: Hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia / hypocalcaemia, uraemia, hypoxia; alcohol withdrawal, cocaine, and drugs that lower the threshold (TCAs, tramadol).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: What is the difference between a provoked seizure and epilepsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: A provoked seizure has an acute reversible cause (glucose, sodium, alcohol, drugs) — treat the cause. Epilepsy is a tendency to recurrent, unprovoked seizures.
A transient focal weakness (typically a limb) after a focal seizure, resolving over minutes to hours — not a stroke, but a post-ictal phenomenon.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: What is the role of an EEG in diagnosing epilepsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: It supports classification but does not make the diagnosis — a normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy, and incidental abnormalities can mislead. Epilepsy is a clinical diagnosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: What are absence seizures and who gets them?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: Brief (<10 s) episodes of vacant staring with abrupt onset and recovery, often many times a day, in children; may be provoked by hyperventilation, with 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: What investigations are used after a first seizure?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back:
• An eyewitness account
  • bloods (glucose, U&E / Na, Ca, toxicology)
  • ECG (to exclude cardiac syncope / long QT)
  • and MRI brain for focal or first-seizure work-up
  • with EEG to classify

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: What driving advice follows a first unprovoked seizure (UK)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back: The patient must stop driving and inform the DVLA; a Group 1 licence generally requires being seizure-free for 6 months after a single seizure (longer with epilepsy) — give this advice explicitly.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.front: What safety advice should you give someone with epilepsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Seizures.back:
• Avoid unsupervised swimming / baths (shower instead)
  • avoid heights and dangerous machinery
  • take medication regularly
  • avoid sleep deprivation and excess alcohol
  • and follow DVLA rules

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: What is transient loss of consciousness (TLoC), and what are the three broad causes?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back:
A brief, self-limiting loss of consciousness with complete spontaneous recovery. Causes:
  • syncope (reflex / orthostatic / cardiac)
  • epileptic seizure
  • and psychogenic attacks
Transient global cerebral hypoperfusion — a temporary fall in blood flow to the whole brain (from a vasovagal reflex, orthostatic drop or a cardiac cause).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: Which two assessments carry the whole TLoC work-up?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back: The eyewitness history (before / during / after) and a 12-lead ECG — done in every patient with TLoC.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: What are the cardiac red flags in TLoC?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back:
• Syncope on exertion or lying flat
  • palpitations beforehand
  • no prodrome
  • a family history of sudden cardiac death <40
  • known structural heart disease
  • or an abnormal ECG

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: What are the '3 Ps' of vasovagal syncope?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back:
• Posture (prolonged standing)
  • a Provoking trigger (pain, emotion, heat, sight of blood)
  • and a Prodrome (nausea, sweating, tunnel vision)
Reflex syncope triggered by a specific act — micturition, coughing, swallowing or defecation — through a vagal reflex.
A fall of ≥20 mmHg systolic (or ≥10 mmHg diastolic) within 3 minutes of standing, with symptoms of cerebral hypoperfusion.

• Drugs (antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha-blockers, nitrates)
  • volume depletion (bleeding, dehydration)
  • and autonomic failure (diabetes, Parkinson’s, ageing)

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: How do you distinguish an epileptic seizure from syncope?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back: Seizure: lateral tongue-bite, prolonged post-ictal confusion, cyanosis, aura. Syncope: upright trigger, prodrome, pallor and rapid recovery (brief myoclonic jerks may still occur).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: Which features do NOT reliably distinguish a seizure from syncope?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back: Urinary incontinence and a few brief myoclonic jerks occur in both — do not rely on them. Use the lateral tongue-bite and prolonged post-ictal confusion, which favour a seizure.
Aortic stenosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (outflow obstruction), and exercise-induced arrhythmias — exertional syncope is a red flag.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: Which ECG abnormalities are important to spot after TLoC?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back:
• Long QT
  • Brugada
  • complete or bifascicular heart block
  • ventricular tachycardia
  • WPW (delta wave)
  • and signs of ischaemia or a prior MI
An exaggerated vagal response to carotid sinus stimulation (head-turning, tight collars, shaving) causing bradycardia / hypotension and syncope, typically in older patients.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: What features suggest a psychogenic (functional) cause of apparent TLoC?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back:
• Prolonged episodes
  • eyes closed and resisted
  • situational occurrence
  • absence of injury
  • and no true post-event confusion or acidosis

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: What bedside measurement is essential when orthostatic hypotension is suspected?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back: A lying and standing blood pressure — measure supine, then after 1 and 3 minutes of standing, looking for a symptomatic drop.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: What targeted investigations are used for suspected cardiac syncope?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back:
• Echocardiography (structural disease / murmur)
  • ambulatory ECG or an implantable loop recorder for intermittent arrhythmia
  • and exercise testing where relevant

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: What driving advice applies after TLoC (UK, Group 1)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back: It depends on the cause — e.g. a simple faint with clear triggers usually needs no restriction, but unexplained or likely-cardiac syncope, or a suspected seizure, requires stopping driving and informing the DVLA.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.front: What must be excluded before labelling an event as TLoC?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Transient Loss of C.back:
The mimics:
  • hypoglycaemia
  • alcohol / drug intoxication
  • head trauma
  • and a mechanical fall without loss of consciousness

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: How does the location of a lesion in the visual pathway relate to the field defect?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back:
• A monocular defect is pre-chiasmal (retina / optic nerve)
  • a bitemporal hemianopia is at the chiasm
  • a homonymous defect is retrochiasmal (tract / radiation / occipital cortex)
Compression at the optic chiasm — most often a pituitary macroadenoma (from below) or a craniopharyngioma (from above).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: What is a homonymous hemianopia and where is the lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back: Loss of the same half of the field in both eyes — from a retrochiasmal lesion (optic tract, radiation or occipital cortex) on the opposite side to the field loss.
An occipital (cortical) lesion, usually a posterior cerebral artery stroke — the macular representation has a dual blood supply, so central vision is spared.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: What is the 'PITS' rule for quadrantanopias?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back:
• Parietal lesions cause an Inferior quadrantanopia
  • Temporal lesions (Meyer’s loop) cause a Superior quadrantanopia

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: What is a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) and what does it signify?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back: On the swinging-light test the affected pupil dilates when the light swings to it — it signifies an optic nerve or extensive retinal lesion (e.g. optic neuritis, CRAO).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: What are the features of optic neuritis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back: Painful monocular visual loss (worse on eye movement), a central scotoma, colour desaturation (especially red) and an RAPD — often the first presentation of MS.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: How does central retinal artery occlusion present?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back: Sudden, painless, profound monocular loss with an RAPD; fundoscopy shows a pale retina with a cherry-red spot — an ocular emergency.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: Why must giant cell arteritis be excluded in sudden monocular visual loss?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back: GCA causes arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy / CRAO and, untreated, can blind the other eye — check ESR / CRP and start high-dose steroids immediately if suspected.
A transient, painless monocular visual loss (a ‘curtain’ coming down) that recovers — a form of TIA from retinal emboli; investigate as a stroke risk.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: What visual field pattern does chronic open-angle glaucoma cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back: A gradual arcuate scotoma progressing to peripheral (tunnel) vision loss, with a preserved central field until late; associated with raised intraocular pressure and disc cupping.
Flashes and floaters followed by a curtain or shadow descending across the field — a painless loss needing urgent ophthalmology referral.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: How does a defect respecting the vertical vs horizontal meridian help localise it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back:
• A defect respecting the vertical meridian is neurological (chiasm or behind)
  • one respecting the horizontal meridian (altitudinal) is retinal / optic-nerve vascular (e.g. AION)
Sudden haemorrhage / infarction of a pituitary tumour — thunderclap headache, a bitemporal defect, ophthalmoplegia and hypopituitarism; an endocrine and neurosurgical emergency.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: How are visual fields assessed at the bedside and formally?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back:
• Confrontation testing (each eye separately, quadrant by quadrant, often with a red pin) at the bedside
  • formal automated perimetry (e.g. Humphrey) to map and quantify the defect
A lesion of the macula (e.g. age-related macular degeneration) or the optic nerve (e.g. optic neuritis) — central vision and acuity are affected.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: Which investigations are used for a chiasmal (bitemporal) field defect?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back: MRI of the pituitary / chiasm and a full pituitary hormone profile (to detect a secreting adenoma and hypopituitarism).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.front: Why does a pituitary macroadenoma classically affect the upper fields first?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Visual Field Defect.back: It compresses the chiasm from below, hitting the inferonasal fibres first — these carry the superior temporal fields, so the upper outer quadrants go first.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: What is the first step in assessing diplopia, and why?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back:
Cover one eye:
  • if the double vision persists it is monocular (an ocular / refractive cause)
  • if it resolves it is binocular (the eyes are misaligned — a neurological cause)
An ocular / refractive problem in the affected eye — cataract, astigmatism, dry eye, corneal disease or a dislocated lens; it does not come from a cranial-nerve palsy and is corrected by a pinhole.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: What are the possible sites of a lesion causing binocular diplopia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back:
• A cranial nerve (III, IV, VI)
  • the neuromuscular junction (myasthenia)
  • an extraocular muscle / orbit (thyroid eye disease)
  • or the brainstem (e.g. internuclear ophthalmoplegia)
Ptosis, the eye held ‘down and out’, and (if the pupil is involved) a fixed dilated pupil; there is diplopia in most directions of gaze.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: What is the 'pupil rule' in a third-nerve palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back:
• Pupil-involving (dilated, unreactive) = compressive (aneurysm) — a surgical emergency, because the parasympathetic fibres run on the surface / outside of the nerve and are caught early
  • Pupil-sparing = microvascular (diabetes / hypertension), which spares the surface fibres

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: Which thiamine-responsive cause of ophthalmoplegia must not be missed?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: Wernicke’s encephalopathy — ophthalmoplegia (classically a VI palsy / conjugate gaze palsy with nystagmus) plus confusion and ataxia, in alcohol excess or malnutrition; give IV thiamine urgently.
Vertical / torsional diplopia that is worse looking down (reading, descending stairs); the patient adopts a compensatory head tilt away from the affected side.
Horizontal diplopia with failed abduction of the affected eye, worse on looking toward that side and at distance; the eye is slightly adducted at rest.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: Why can an isolated sixth-nerve palsy be a 'false-localising' sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: The abducens nerve has a long intracranial course and is stretched by raised intracranial pressure, so a VI palsy can occur without a lesion in its own territory.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: What are the features of myasthenia gravis affecting the eyes?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: Fatigable, variable diplopia and ptosis that are worse in the evening / on sustained gaze, with a normal pupil; confirmed with anti-AChR antibodies and repetitive nerve stimulation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: What is internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) and what causes it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus: failed adduction of one eye with nystagmus in the abducting eye on lateral gaze — classically MS (or brainstem stroke).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: What features suggest thyroid eye disease as a cause of diplopia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: Restrictive diplopia (worse on up-gaze) with proptosis, lid retraction / lag and injection — one of the commonest causes of diplopia in adults; check thyroid function.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: What is a cavernous sinus lesion's effect on eye movements?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: It can affect cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and VI together (± proptosis and a Horner’s), because they all pass through the sinus — causing a complex ophthalmoplegia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: How do you test for and localise binocular diplopia at the bedside?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: Assess ocular movements in the ‘H’ pattern and a cover test; the diplopia is maximal in the direction of action of the weak muscle, and the outer image belongs to the affected eye.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: Which painful ophthalmoplegia in an older patient must not be missed?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: Giant cell arteritis — it can cause ischaemic ocular motor palsies and threatens vision; check ESR / CRP and start steroids if suspected.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: What investigations are used for a third-nerve palsy with pupil involvement?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: Urgent CT / CT angiography (or MRA) to exclude a posterior communicating artery aneurysm — imaging takes priority over blood tests.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: How is a microvascular ocular motor palsy expected to behave?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: It is usually pupil-sparing and painless or mildly painful in a diabetic / hypertensive patient, and typically recovers spontaneously over 3 months.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.front: What is the ice-pack test used for?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Diplopia.back: A bedside test for myasthenic ptosis: cooling the lid with an ice pack for ~2 minutes improves the ptosis (cold slows acetylcholinesterase), supporting myasthenia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What triad of symptoms do bulbar and pseudobulbar palsy share?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back:
• Dysarthria (slurred speech)
  • dysphagia (choking / nasal regurgitation)
  • and dysphonia (weak / nasal / strangled voice)
— from dysfunction of cranial nerves IX–XII.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: Which cranial nerves are involved in bulbar/pseudobulbar palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back:
The lower cranial nerves:
  • IX (glossopharyngeal)
  • X (vagus)
  • XI (accessory)
  • and XII (hypoglossal).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What is the fundamental difference between bulbar and pseudobulbar palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back:
• Bulbar palsy is a lower motor neurone lesion (medullary nuclei / nerves)
  • pseudobulbar palsy is an upper motor neurone lesion (bilateral corticobulbar tracts).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What are the tongue and jaw jerk findings in bulbar (LMN) palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: A flaccid, wasted, fasciculating tongue with a normal or absent jaw jerk and an absent gag; speech is nasal.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What are the tongue and jaw jerk findings in pseudobulbar (UMN) palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: A small, spastic, immobile tongue (no wasting or fasciculation) with a brisk jaw jerk and brisk gag; speech is strangled / ‘hot-potato’.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: Which feature of affect is characteristic of pseudobulbar palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: Emotional lability — pathological / involuntary crying or laughing, out of keeping with the situation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What are the common causes of bulbar palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back:
• Motor neurone disease
  • Guillain-Barré syndrome
  • myasthenia gravis
  • brainstem infarction
  • syringobulbia and poliomyelitis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What are the common causes of pseudobulbar palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back:
• Bilateral strokes
  • multiple sclerosis
  • motor neurone disease
  • and high brainstem lesions
— anything affecting the corticobulbar tracts bilaterally.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: Why can motor neurone disease cause a 'mixed' bulbar picture?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: MND affects both upper and lower motor neurones, so signs can co-exist — e.g. a brisk jaw jerk with a wasted, fasciculating tongue.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What is the immediate safety priority in a patient with bulbar symptoms?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: Swallow safety — if unsafe (choking, wet voice, nasal regurgitation) keep the patient nil by mouth, get an urgent SALT assessment and prevent aspiration pneumonia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: How is respiratory compromise monitored in bulbar Guillain-Barré or myasthenia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: By serial forced vital capacity (FVC) — it falls before the oxygen saturations drop, so a declining FVC warns of impending respiratory failure and the need for ventilation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What speech quality is typical of pseudobulbar palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: A strained, strangled, ‘hot-potato’ (spastic) voice — contrasted with the nasal, weak speech of bulbar palsy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: Which investigations help identify the cause of a bulbar/pseudobulbar palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back:
• MRI brain / brainstem
  • EMG / nerve conduction studies (MND, GBS)
  • anti-AChR antibodies (myasthenia)
  • and FVC monitoring
  • SALT ± video-fluoroscopy for the swallow.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What examination confirms an unsafe swallow at the bedside?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: A bedside swallow test (a sip of water) showing cough, choking or a wet voice — then formal SALT assessment ± video-fluoroscopy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: How is nutrition maintained when the swallow is unsafe?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: Nil by mouth initially with NG tube feeding, progressing to a PEG (gastrostomy) if dysphagia is prolonged (e.g. in MND).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: Which acute vascular event causes a sudden bulbar palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: A brainstem (medullary) stroke — e.g. lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome — presenting with acute dysphagia, dysarthria and crossed signs.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: What ascending, areflexic weakness with bulbar involvement suggests which diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: Guillain-Barré syndrome — an ascending, symmetrical, areflexic weakness that can involve bulbar and respiratory muscles; monitor FVC.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.front: Why is bulbar-onset motor neurone disease significant prognostically?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Bulbar & Pseudobulb.back: Bulbar-onset MND has a worse prognosis — early dysphagia and aspiration risk shorten survival compared with limb-onset disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What is the difference between dysarthria and dysphasia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back:
• Dysarthria is a motor disorder of articulation (slurred speech, language intact)
  • dysphasia (aphasia) is a disorder of language itself (comprehension, naming, repetition or fluency).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: Which three bedside tasks separate dysarthria from dysphasia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back:
• Name an object
  • follow a spoken command
  • and repeat a phrase.
Intact language with slurred sound = dysarthria; failure of any = dysphasia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: In which hemisphere does dysphasia usually localise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back: The dominant hemisphere (the left in almost all right-handers and most left-handers).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What are the features of Broca's (expressive) dysphasia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back:
• Non-fluent, effortful speech with intact comprehension
  • the patient is aware and frustrated
  • repetition is impaired.
Lesion in the inferior frontal gyrus (frontal lobe).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What are the features of Wernicke's (receptive) dysphasia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back:
• Fluent but nonsensical speech (paraphasias, neologisms) with poor comprehension
  • the patient is often unaware
  • repetition impaired.
Lesion in the temporal lobe.
Fluent speech with intact comprehension but impaired repetition, due to a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus connecting Wernicke's and Broca's areas.
Impairment of all language modalities — fluency, comprehension, naming and repetition — from a large dominant-hemisphere (usually MCA) lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: Why is an acute dysphasia or dysarthria a red flag?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back: It is the ‘S’ of FAST — a stroke until proven otherwise; it needs an urgent CT and consideration of thrombolysis / thrombectomy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What are the reversible mimics of a stroke causing speech disturbance?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back:
• Hypoglycaemia
  • a post-ictal Todd’s phenomenon
  • and a peripheral facial (Bell’s) palsy
— always check the glucose.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What speech pattern is typical of cerebellar dysarthria?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back: Scanning / staccato, slurred, irregular speech with abnormal separation of syllables — part of the cerebellar syndrome (DANISH).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What speech pattern is typical of extrapyramidal (Parkinsonian) dysarthria?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back: Quiet, monotonous, hypophonic and festinant (hurried) speech, reflecting hypokinesia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What speech pattern is typical of spastic (pseudobulbar) dysarthria?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back: A strained, strangled voice from bilateral upper motor neurone (corticobulbar) involvement, often with a brisk jaw jerk and emotional lability.
It causes fatigable dysarthria — the voice becomes more slurred / nasal the longer the patient talks, and recovers with rest.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What is dysphonia, and how does it differ from dysarthria?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back: Dysphonia is a disorder of voice production (volume / quality — e.g. a hoarse or weak voice, often from vocal-cord / recurrent laryngeal problems), whereas dysarthria is disordered articulation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What investigations are used for a subacute, progressive dysphasia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back: MRI brain to look for a tumour, abscess or demyelination, since a gradually progressive language disturbance is not typical of a single stroke.
Relatively isolated difficulty naming objects (word-finding pauses, circumlocution) with otherwise fluent speech and good comprehension.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What is the role of speech and language therapy (SALT) in speech disturbance?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back: SALT assesses and rehabilitates communication and, crucially, the safety of swallowing — important in stroke and bulbar disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.front: What speech pattern is typical of flaccid (bulbar / LMN) dysarthria?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dysarthria & Dyspha.back: Nasal, breathy speech with nasal escape, from lower motor neurone weakness of the palate, tongue and larynx — e.g. bulbar palsy, MND or myasthenia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: What is the key question when assessing cranial nerve palsies?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back:
How many nerves, and grouped how?
  • A single nerve = mononeuropathy
  • an anatomical cluster = one site (brainstem, cavernous sinus, CP angle, jugular foramen)
  • diffuse = a systemic cause.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: Which cranial nerves pass through the cavernous sinus?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: III, IV, V1 (and V2), VI plus the sympathetic fibres — so a cavernous sinus lesion gives a complex ophthalmoplegia ± Horner’s and proptosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: Which cranial nerves are affected at the cerebellopontine angle?
