signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: V, VII and VIII (± cerebellar signs) — classically a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: Which cranial nerves exit through the jugular foramen?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: IX, X and XI — a jugular foramen lesion affects these together (Vernet’s syndrome).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: How does the tongue deviate in a hypoglossal (XII) lower motor neurone palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: The tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion on protrusion (the weak genioglossus fails to push it across), with wasting / fasciculation if LMN.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: What are the functions of the trigeminal nerve (V)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back:
• Facial sensation (three divisions)
  • the muscles of mastication
  • and the afferent limb of the corneal reflex.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: What is a false-localising sign, and which cranial nerve classically shows it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: A sign implying a lesion elsewhere than the true site: an isolated sixth-nerve palsy from raised intracranial pressure (its long intracranial course is stretched).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: Which cranial nerve palsy with a dilated pupil is a surgical emergency?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: A third-nerve palsy with a fixed dilated pupil (and pain) — a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until angiography proves otherwise.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: What causes a microvascular cranial nerve palsy and how does it behave?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: Diabetes / hypertension → a painless, usually pupil-sparing III / IV / VI palsy that recovers over ~3 months.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: What are the causes of a bilateral facial (VII) nerve palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back:
Think systemic:
  • Lyme disease
  • sarcoidosis
  • Guillain-Barré syndrome
  • and (rarely) myasthenia
— bilateral involvement points away from a single focal lesion.
Herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion: a lower motor neurone facial (VII) palsy with painful vesicles in the ear / palate ± hearing loss and vertigo.
A Guillain-Barré variant — the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia (anti-GQ1b antibodies), often post-infective.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: How do you distinguish an upper from a lower motor neurone facial (VII) palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: Forehead sparing (able to wrinkle) = UMN (e.g. stroke), because the upper face has bilateral cortical supply; whole hemiface weak = LMN (e.g. Bell’s).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: What is the classic cause and features of a cerebellopontine angle tumour?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: A vestibular schwannoma: progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss & tinnitus, then a reduced V (corneal reflex) ± ataxia; the facial nerve (VII) is relatively resistant and tends to be involved late.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: How does malignant otitis externa present with cranial nerve palsies?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: In an elderly diabetic / immunocompromised patient: severe ear pain and discharge with progressive lower cranial nerve (VII, IX–XII) palsies — a Pseudomonas skull-base osteomyelitis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: Which investigation is targeted to the localised site of a multi-nerve palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: MRI of the relevant region (brainstem, cavernous sinus with MRV, or the internal auditory meatus for a CP-angle lesion), ± CT / CT angiography for an aneurysm.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: What CSF finding supports carcinomatous (neoplastic) meningitis causing multiple cranial nerve palsies?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: Malignant cells on CSF cytology (often needing repeated large-volume LPs), with raised protein and low glucose.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.front: Which cranial nerve is tested by the corneal reflex, and what are its limbs?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Cranial Nerve Palsi.back: The afferent limb is V (trigeminal, V1) and the efferent limb is VII (facial, orbicularis oculi).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: What single sign distinguishes an upper from a lower motor neurone facial weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: Forehead sparing. UMN spares the forehead (bilateral cortical supply — the patient can wrinkle the brow); LMN weakens the whole hemiface, including the forehead.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: Why is the forehead spared in an upper motor neurone facial palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: The upper face has bilateral cortical (corticobulbar) supply, so a unilateral UMN lesion still drives the forehead from the other hemisphere; the lower face has only contralateral supply and is weak.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: What is the typical cause of an UMN facial weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: A stroke (or other contralateral cortical / corticobulbar lesion) — usually with other focal signs (arm weakness, speech); acute onset means FAST and urgent imaging.

An acute, unilateral lower motor neurone facial (VII) palsy of unknown cause — a diagnosis of exclusion; may have post-auricular pain, hyperacusis and altered taste (anterior two-thirds of the tongue).
Oral corticosteroids within 72 hours (e.g. prednisolone) improve recovery, plus eye protection; grade with House-Brackmann. Most recover over weeks to months.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: Why is eye protection essential in a lower motor neurone facial palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: The patient cannot close the eye, risking exposure keratopathy / corneal ulceration — give lubricating drops by day and ointment + taping at night.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: What is Ramsay Hunt syndrome and how does it differ from Bell's palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: Herpes zoster of the geniculate ganglion: an LMN facial palsy with painful vesicles in the ear / palate ± hearing loss and vertigo; treated with aciclovir + steroids (worse prognosis than Bell’s).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: Why is a bilateral facial weakness never simply 'Bell's palsy'?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: Bilateral involvement points to a systemic cause — Guillain-Barré syndrome, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis or myasthenia — and must be investigated.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: Which otological causes can produce a lower motor neurone facial palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: Middle-ear disease — otitis media, cholesteatoma and malignant (necrotising) otitis externa (elderly diabetic) — because VII runs through the temporal bone.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: Why must a parotid mass with facial weakness be taken seriously?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: The facial nerve runs through the parotid gland, so a slowly progressive facial palsy with a parotid lump suggests a parotid malignancy until proven otherwise.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: What features suggest a facial weakness is NOT Bell's palsy (red flags)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back:
• Forehead sparing (UMN)
  • bilateral weakness
  • slowly progressive onset
  • failure to recover
  • recurrent episodes
  • or an associated parotid mass / ear disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: How does myasthenia gravis affect the face?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: It causes fatigable bilateral facial and eyelid weakness (with ptosis / diplopia) that worsens with use — a neuromuscular-junction cause, not a nerve lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: What is the House-Brackmann scale used for?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: Grading the severity of a facial nerve palsy (grade I normal to VI complete paralysis) — useful for documenting baseline and tracking recovery.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: How does Lyme disease cause facial weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: Lyme neuroborreliosis can cause a facial (VII) palsy, sometimes bilateral, often with a history of tick exposure or erythema migrans; treat with antibiotics (e.g. doxycycline).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: Which investigations are appropriate for an atypical or non-recovering facial palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back:
• MRI (UMN signs, progressive, recurrent, non-recovering)
  • bloods / serology for Lyme and sarcoid
  • and CT temporal bone for otological causes
  • anti-AChR if fatigable.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: What non-motor symptoms can accompany a lower motor neurone facial palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back:
• Hyperacusis (loss of stapedius)
  • loss of taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani)
  • reduced tear / saliva production and post-auricular pain.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: What is the prognosis of Bell's palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: Most (~70–85%) recover fully over weeks to months, especially with early steroids; incomplete palsies do best. Poorer recovery with complete paralysis, older age or Ramsay Hunt.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.front: How can a cerebellopontine angle lesion cause facial weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Facial Weakness.back: A vestibular schwannoma (or other CP-angle tumour) compresses VII alongside VIII and V — a lower motor neurone facial weakness with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss ± an absent corneal reflex; image with MRI of the internal auditory meatus.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: Why is watching a patient walk such a useful bedside test?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: The gait pattern localises the lesion — observe stand, initiation, base width, arm swing, symmetry, turning and tandem (heel-to-toe) walking before formally examining.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: What is a hemiplegic gait and what causes it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: One leg held extended and circumducted (swung out in an arc), with a flexed arm — a unilateral upper motor neurone lesion, classically after a stroke.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: What is a spastic (scissoring) gait and what causes it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: Stiff, adducted legs that cross / scissor with toe-walking — a bilateral UMN lesion (cord / cervical myelopathy, MS, or cerebral palsy).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: How does a cerebellar ataxic gait present?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: A broad (wide-based), unsteady, staggering gait; the patient cannot walk heel-to-toe and veers toward the side of the lesion; Romberg is negative.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: How does a sensory ataxic gait present, and what is the key discriminator?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: A high-stepping, stamping gait; the patient watches their feet and is much worse in the dark — Romberg is positive (loss of proprioception).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: What does Romberg's test distinguish between ataxic gaits?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: Romberg positive (falls on eye closure) = sensory ataxia; a cerebellar patient is unsteady with eyes open or shut, so Romberg is negative.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: What are the features of a Parkinsonian gait?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back:
• Shuffling, small steps
  • stooped posture
  • reduced arm swing
  • festination (hurrying)
  • difficulty initiating and freezing
  • with slow multi-step turns.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: What is an apraxic ('magnetic') gait and what does it suggest?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: Feet appear stuck to the floor with difficulty initiating, yet leg movements are near-normal when tested on the bed — a frontal / normal-pressure hydrocephalus gait.
Gait apraxia + urinary incontinence + cognitive decline (‘wet, wobbly, wacky’) — a treatable cause; ventriculomegaly on imaging and improvement after a CSF tap test / shunt.
Foot drop — weak ankle dorsiflexion, so the foot is lifted high and slaps down; from a common peroneal nerve, L5 root or peripheral neuropathy lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: What is a waddling gait and what causes it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: A broad, rolling gait with the pelvis dropping on the swing side (Trendelenburg) — from proximal muscle (hip girdle) weakness, e.g. a myopathy.
A pain-avoiding gait with a shortened stance phase on the painful leg — the patient spends as little time as possible weight-bearing on it.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: When is a gait disturbance a surgical emergency?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: When accompanied by bladder / bowel disturbance, back pain or a sensory level — suggesting cord compression or cauda equina syndrome, needing urgent MRI and decompression.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: Which chronic causes of gait disturbance are important because they are treatable?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus (shunt) and B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) — both reversible if caught early.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: What examination findings accompany an upper motor neurone gait?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back:
• Increased tone (spasticity)
  • hyperreflexia
  • upgoing plantars
  • and a pyramidal pattern of weakness (weak extensors in the arm, weak flexors in the leg).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: How does cerebral palsy typically affect gait?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: Commonly a spastic (diplegic) scissoring, toe-walking gait from a non-progressive UMN lesion of the developing brain.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: What investigations are used for an unexplained gait disorder?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back:
• MRI brain / whole spine (stroke, cord compression, NPH, MS)
  • B12
  • glucose / HbA1c and TFTs
  • and nerve conduction studies for suspected foot drop / neuropathy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.front: Why is gait assessment central to the elderly faller?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Gait Abnormalities.back: Falls are usually multifactorial; gait & balance assessment (with a lying/standing BP and medication review) identifies reversible contributors and reduces fracture / subdural risk.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: Why are falls in older people described as 'multifactorial'?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: They result from the interaction of intrinsic factors (gait/balance, vision, cognition, postural hypotension, arrhythmia, sarcopenia/frailty), medications and environmental hazards — rarely a single cause.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What is the strongest single predictor of a future fall?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: A previous fall — which is why every fall in an older person warrants a full multifactorial assessment.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What are the three broad categories a fall should be triaged into?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back:
• Mechanical (trip / slip)
  • syncopal (loss of consciousness — work up as TLoC)
  • or a ‘found on floor / off legs’ presentation of acute illness.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What question must always be asked about a fall, and why?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: ‘Was it really a faint?’ — a collapse with no warning, palpitations or on exertion may be cardiac syncope / arrhythmia (do an ECG), which is easily mislabelled a trip and carries a risk of sudden death.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: Which medication classes most increase falls risk?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back:
• Sedatives / hypnotics (benzodiazepines, Z-drugs)
  • antipsychotics, opioids
  • antihypertensives / diuretics / nitrates (postural drop)
  • anticholinergics
  • and hypoglycaemics (insulin / sulfonylureas).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What tool guides rationalising medications in older fallers?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: STOPP/START criteria — used to deprescribe inappropriate (falls-risk) drugs and start indicated ones; polypharmacy itself is a falls risk.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: Why should a head injury from a fall on an anticoagulant prompt a CT head?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: There is a high risk of an intracranial (subdural) haematoma; anticoagulated / antiplatelet patients need a low threshold for CT even after apparently minor trauma.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What are the complications of a 'long lie' after a fall?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: Rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury (raised CK), pressure injury, hypothermia and dehydration — check a CK and U&E.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: How does a fractured neck of femur present after a fall?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: A shortened, externally rotated leg with hip pain and inability to weight-bear; confirm with a hip X-ray (MRI if occult but strongly suspected).

Ask older people whether they have fallen in the past year. Offer a multifactorial falls assessment to anyone who
  • presents for medical care because of a fall
  • reports recurrent falls
  • or has a gait / balance abnormality.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What is measured with a lying and standing blood pressure, and what is significant?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: Orthostatic (postural) hypotension — a fall of ≥20 mmHg systolic (or ≥10 diastolic) within 3 minutes of standing, often drug-related.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What bedside test screens gait and balance in a faller?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: The Timed Up and Go (rise from a chair, walk 3 m, turn, return, sit) — a prolonged time (or unsteadiness / turn-180 difficulty) flags falls risk.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What is the 'fear of falling' cycle?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: After a fall, loss of confidence leads to reduced activity, causing deconditioning and muscle loss, which increases the risk of further falls.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What are the key components of a multifactorial falls assessment?
Which interventions reduce falls and fall-related harm?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back:
• Strength & balance training
  • deprescribing falls-risk drugs
  • bone protection (calcium / vitamin D ± bisphosphonate)
  • home-hazard / OT review
  • vision correction and appropriate footwear.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: How is bone-fracture risk assessed after a fragility fracture or recurrent falls?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: With a FRAX score ± DEXA scan; a fragility fracture (from a standing-height fall) itself signals osteoporosis and prompts bone-protection treatment.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: Why is an ECG a key investigation in an older faller?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: To detect an arrhythmia or conduction disorder (e.g. complete heart block, long QT) as an occult cardiac / syncopal cause — do it whenever a faint or cardiac cause is possible.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.front: What simple bloods are useful in the faller, especially after a long lie?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Falls in the Elderl.back: FBC, U&E, glucose, calcium and bone profile, and a creatine kinase (CK) if a long lie is suspected (rhabdomyolysis).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: Which two muscles hold up the upper eyelid, and what supplies each?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: Levator palpebrae superioris (cranial nerve III) and Müller’s muscle (sympathetic) — so ptosis localises to CN III, the sympathetic chain, the NMJ or the muscle itself.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: How does the pupil help classify ptosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back:
• Dilated pupil → CN III palsy
  • small pupil (miosis) → Horner’s syndrome
  • normal pupil → myasthenia or a myogenic cause.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: What are the eyelid and eye features of a third-nerve palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: Complete ptosis with the eye ‘down and out’ and diplopia; ± a dilated pupil (if the pupil is involved).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: What is the 'pupil rule' in a third-nerve palsy causing ptosis?
What is the triad of Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back:
• Partial ptosis (weak Müller’s muscle)
  • miosis (small pupil)
  • and anhidrosis (± apparent enophthalmos)
— from a sympathetic-chain lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: Why is the ptosis of Horner's syndrome only partial?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: Because it is due to loss of Müller’s muscle (a small sympathetic lid elevator) — the main levator (CN III) still works, so the lid only droops slightly.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: How is a Horner's syndrome localised along the sympathetic chain?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back:
• Central (brainstem / cord, e.g. stroke) — anhidrosis of the whole side
  • preganglionic (T1 apex, e.g. Pancoast) — facial anhidrosis
  • postganglionic (carotid, e.g. dissection / cluster) — little / no anhidrosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: What are the dangerous causes of a Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: Carotid dissection (painful, acute — young patient with neck / face pain) and a Pancoast (apical lung) tumour; both must be actively excluded.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: What are the features of myasthenic ptosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: Fatigable, variable ptosis that is worse in the evening / on sustained up-gaze, often bilateral and asymmetric, with diplopia and a normal pupil.
A bedside test for myasthenic ptosis: applying an ice pack to the closed lid for ~2 minutes improves the ptosis (cold slows acetylcholinesterase).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: What is the commonest cause of ptosis overall?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: Aponeurotic (involutional / senile) ptosis — age-related dehiscence of the levator aponeurosis; usually bilateral, in the elderly, with a high lid crease and good levator function; also contact-lens related.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: What are the features of ptosis in myotonic dystrophy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: Bilateral ptosis with frontal balding, wasted facial / temporalis muscles, grip myotonia (slow release) and cataracts — an autosomal-dominant multisystem disorder.
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia — a mitochondrial disorder causing bilateral ptosis and slowly progressive ophthalmoplegia with little diplopia (both eyes move together as they weaken).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: Which investigation is most urgent for a ptosis with a dilated pupil and pain?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: CT / CT angiography to exclude a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compressing CN III.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: How is a suspected Horner's syndrome confirmed and localised pharmacologically?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: Apraclonidine (or cocaine) drops confirm Horner’s; hydroxyamfetamine drops help separate postganglionic from pre-ganglionic / central lesions.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: What examination confirms a myogenic vs neurogenic ptosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back:
Assess
  • fatigability (myasthenia)
  • the pupil and eye movements (III / Horner’s)
  • and levator function & systemic features (myotonia, ophthalmoplegia) for a myogenic cause.
An apparent droop without levator weakness — e.g. dermatochalasis (excess lid skin), a small / sunken eye (enophthalmos, microphthalmos) or brow ptosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.front: Why must the FVC be monitored in a patient with fatigable ptosis and bulbar symptoms?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Ptosis.back: Because myasthenia can progress to a myasthenic crisis with respiratory muscle failure; the FVC falls before the oxygen saturations, warning of the need for ventilation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: How do you decide which pupil is abnormal in anisocoria?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back:
Compare the difference in light vs dark:
  • anisocoria worse in the dark = the small pupil is abnormal (sympathetic / Horner’s)
  • worse in bright light = the large pupil is abnormal (parasympathetic / CN III / Adie’s).
A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) — the affected pupil dilates when the light swings to it — indicating an optic nerve or extensive retinal lesion (an afferent problem, not a size problem).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: What are the pupil features of a third-nerve palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back: A dilated pupil with ptosis and the eye ‘down and out’; a painful, pupil-involving III palsy is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until angiography excludes it.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: What does a fixed dilated pupil with a falling GCS indicate?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back: Uncal (transtentorial) herniation — ‘coning’ — compressing CN III; a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent CT and measures to reduce intracranial pressure.
A large, tonic pupil (typically a young woman) with a poor / slow reaction to light and a slow tonic near response; with absent ankle / knee reflexes it is Holmes-Adie syndrome — benign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: What is the triad and pupil finding of Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back:
• Miosis (small pupil)
  • partial ptosis
  • and anhidrosis
the anisocoria is worse in the dark because the affected pupil cannot dilate (sympathetic lesion).
Small, irregular pupils that accommodate but do not react to light (light-near dissociation), classically bilateral — from neurosyphilis (also diabetes).
A pupil that reacts better to a near target than to light — seen in Argyll Robertson (small, irregular) and Holmes-Adie (large, tonic) pupils; pupil size separates them.
Opioid toxicity (with a low respiratory rate — give naloxone) or a pontine haemorrhage; cholinergic drugs also cause miosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: How do pharmacological drops help identify a dilated pupil's cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back:
• Pilocarpine 0.1% constricts an Adie’s pupil (denervation supersensitivity)
  • pilocarpine 1% constricts a third-nerve pupil but not a pharmacological (atropine) mydriasis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: Why must a painful Horner's syndrome be investigated urgently?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back: It may be a carotid artery dissection (postganglionic, painful, with neck / face pain) — a cause of stroke needing urgent imaging (CT / MR angiography).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: How is a Horner's syndrome confirmed pharmacologically?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back: Apraclonidine (or cocaine) drops confirm Horner’s; hydroxyamfetamine then separates a postganglionic from a preganglionic / central lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: What causes a unilateral fixed dilated pupil that will NOT constrict to pilocarpine 1%?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back: A pharmacological (atropine / mydriatic) mydriasis or a traumatic (iris) mydriasis — the sphincter cannot respond; a true III palsy would constrict to 1%.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: How does the pupil rule apply to a third-nerve palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back:
• Pupil-involving (dilated, unreactive) = compressive (aneurysm) — the parasympathetic fibres run on the surface
  • pupil-sparing = microvascular (diabetes / hypertension).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: What does an RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil) tell you?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back: That the afferent (optic nerve / retinal) pathway on that side is impaired (e.g. optic neuritis, CRAO) — both pupils are equal at rest; the defect only shows on the swinging-light test.

• Afferent: retina → optic nerve (II) → pretectal nuclei (bilateral)
  • efferent: Edinger-Westphal nucleus → parasympathetic CN III → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae
— so light in one eye constricts both (direct & consensual).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.front: What does a bilateral fixed dilated unreactive pupil suggest?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Abnormal Pupils.back: Severe anoxic / midbrain brain injury (e.g. after cardiac arrest, brain death) or an anticholinergic / sympathomimetic drug effect — a grave sign in the unconscious patient.
A small pupil-size difference that is equal in light and dark, with normal reactions and no ptosis — the commonest cause of unequal pupils; benign and needs no investigation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is the first split when classifying a movement disorder?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: Hypokinetic (too little movement — Parkinsonism) vs hyperkinetic (excess movement — chorea, dystonia, myoclonus, tics, hemiballismus, athetosis).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is the triad of Parkinsonism?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back:
• Bradykinesia (essential)
  • rigidity (cogwheel / lead-pipe)
  • and a resting (pill-rolling) tremor
often with postural instability and a shuffling gait.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: How does idiopathic Parkinson's disease differ from drug-induced parkinsonism?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back:
• Parkinson’s is asymmetric with a prominent rest tremor and good levodopa response
  • drug-induced (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) is typically symmetric and improves on stopping the drug.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is chorea?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: Brief, irregular, flowing, dance-like involuntary movements that flit from one body part to another; the patient may incorporate them into semi-purposeful movements (parakinesia).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What are the features of Huntington's disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: An autosomal-dominant CAG trinucleotide-repeat disorder on chromosome 4 (HTT gene; anticipation, full penetrance ≥40 repeats): chorea + progressive cognitive decline and psychiatric change, with a positive family history; caudate atrophy on MRI.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is Sydenham's chorea?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: A post-streptococcal chorea (a major criterion of rheumatic fever), typically in children, often with emotional lability; usually self-limiting.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is dystonia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back:
Sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing twisting, repetitive movements or abnormal postures — e.g.
  • cervical dystonia (torticollis)
  • blepharospasm
  • writer’s cramp.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is an acute dystonic reaction and how is it treated?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: An acute drug-induced dystonia (antipsychotics / metoclopramide) — e.g. oculogyric crisis or torticollis; treated with an anticholinergic (procyclidine / benztropine).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What are tics, and what is Tourette's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back:
• Stereotyped, repetitive movements that are briefly suppressible with a premonitory urge
  • Tourette’s is multiple motor tics plus one or more vocal tics lasting >1 year.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is myoclonus?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: Sudden, brief, shock-like involuntary jerks; causes include metabolic (uraemic / hepatic — asterixis is 'negative' myoclonus), epileptic, and post-hypoxic myoclonus.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is hemiballismus and what causes it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: Violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of one side of the body, from a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus — classically a stroke.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is tardive dyskinesia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: Repetitive orofacial movements (lip-smacking, chewing, tongue protrusion) from long-term dopamine-receptor blockade (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) — often irreversible.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: Why must Wilson's disease be excluded in a young patient with a movement disorder?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back:
It is a treatable cause — copper accumulation can produce tremor, dystonia, parkinsonism or chorea; screen with
  • low serum caeruloplasmin
  • high urinary copper
  • and Kayser-Fleischer rings.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: A life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists: rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability and a raised CK (± altered consciousness); stop the drug and give supportive care ± dantrolene / bromocriptine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What are the 'Parkinson-plus' syndromes?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back:
• Progressive supranuclear palsy (early falls, vertical gaze palsy)
  • multiple system atrophy (autonomic failure)
  • and corticobasal degeneration
— parkinsonism with extra features and a poor levodopa response.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: Which drugs commonly cause movement disorders?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: Dopamine antagonists — antipsychotics and metoclopramide / prochlorperazine (parkinsonism, acute dystonia, tardive dyskinesia, NMS); levodopa causes dyskinesias.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What investigations are used in a young patient with chorea or dystonia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back:
• Caeruloplasmin / copper + slit-lamp (Wilson’s)
  • genetic testing (Huntington’s)
  • MRI brain
  • ASOT / anti-DNase B (Sydenham’s)
  • and an autoimmune screen (SLE / antiphospholipid).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What non-genetic / systemic causes of chorea should be considered?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back:
• Drugs (levodopa, neuroleptics)
  • SLE / antiphospholipid syndrome
  • pregnancy (chorea gravidarum)
  • thyrotoxicosis
  • polycythaemia and Wilson’s disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is the standard drug for symptomatic control of chorea (e.g. in Huntington's)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: Tetrabenazine (a dopamine-depleting agent); antipsychotics (e.g. risperidone, olanzapine) are alternatives.Treat the underlying cause where possible.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.front: What is restless legs syndrome and what should you check for?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Movement Disorders.back: An urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, worse at rest / in the evening and relieved by movement. Check for iron deficiency (ferritin), and consider pregnancy, renal failure and neuropathy.Rx: correct iron; dopamine agonists or gabapentinoids.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: What is the triad of Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back:
Ipsilateral
  • partial ptosis
  • miosis (small pupil)
  • and anhidrosis (reduced sweating)
  • often with apparent enophthalmos
— from interruption of the oculosympathetic pathway.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: In Horner's syndrome, when is the anisocoria most obvious and why?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: In the dark: the sympathetically-denervated pupil cannot dilate, so the difference is greatest in dim light (with a slow dilation lag).The pupil still reacts normally to light and near.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: Why is the ptosis in Horner's only partial, unlike a third-nerve palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: Horner’s weakens only Müller’s muscle (sympathetic), giving a few mm of droop; the levator palpebrae (CN III) is intact.A III palsy weakens levator and causes complete ptosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: What is 'upside-down ptosis' in Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: Slight elevation of the lower lid (from weakness of the inferior tarsal muscle) alongside the upper-lid droop, narrowing the palpebral fissure and mimicking enophthalmos.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: Outline the three-neuron oculosympathetic pathway.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back:
• First-order (central): hypothalamus → brainstem → C8–T2 (ciliospinal centre).
  • Second-order (preganglionic): C8–T2 → over the lung apex → superior cervical ganglion.
  • Third-order (postganglionic): ganglion → along the ICA → orbit.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: What are the causes of a FIRST-order (central) Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back:
Brainstem / cord lesions:
  • lateral medullary (Wallenberg) stroke
  • multiple sclerosis
  • syringomyelia
  • cervical cord tumour.
Anhidrosis affects the whole ipsilateral face and body.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: What are the causes of a SECOND-order (preganglionic) Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back:
Lesions over the lung apex / neck:
  • Pancoast apical lung tumour
  • thyroid or neck surgery / trauma
  • cervical rib
  • lower brachial-plexus (T1) lesions.
Anhidrosis affects the face only.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: What are the causes of a THIRD-order (postganglionic) Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back:
Lesions along the ICA:
  • carotid dissection (painful)
  • cluster headache
  • cavernous-sinus lesions
  • carotid aneurysm.
There is little or no anhidrosis (facial sweat fibres branch off earlier).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: How does the distribution of anhidrosis help localise a Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back:
• Whole half of the body → first-order (central)
  • face only → second-order (preganglionic)
  • little or none → third-order (postganglionic).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: How does apraclonidine confirm Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: The denervated pupil develops alpha-1 supersensitivity, so apraclonidine (a weak alpha-1 agonist) dilates it and reverses the anisocoria; the normal pupil is unaffected or constricts slightly.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: What is the cocaine test in Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: Cocaine blocks noradrenaline reuptake, so a normal pupil dilates but a Horner’s pupil (no sympathetic tone / no NA release) fails to dilate, confirming the diagnosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: How does hydroxyamfetamine localise a Horner's lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: It releases stored noradrenaline from the third-order neuron, so it dilates a pre-ganglionic (first/second-order) Horner’s but fails in a post-ganglionic (third-order) lesion, where that neuron is damaged.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: Why must a painful, acute Horner's syndrome be investigated urgently?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: It suggests a carotid (or vertebral) artery dissection — postganglionic, with neck / face pain — a cause of stroke needing urgent CT / MR angiography and antithrombotic treatment.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: What is a Pancoast tumour and its features?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: An apical lung tumour invading the sympathetic chain and lower brachial plexus: preganglionic Horner’s + T1 hand wasting + arm pain, often with weight loss — needs a CXR / CT chest.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: What does Horner's syndrome in a child suggest, and what sign supports it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: Neuroblastoma (or birth trauma) — check urinary catecholamines (VMA/HVA) and image the chest / abdomen. Congenital Horner’s classically causes iris heterochromia (a paler ipsilateral iris).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: What is lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: A first-order Horner’s from a PICA / vertebral stroke: ipsilateral Horner’s, facial sensory loss, ataxia, vertigo and bulbar signs with contralateral body pain/temperature loss (crossed pattern).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: Why does congenital Horner's syndrome cause iris heterochromia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: Sympathetic innervation is needed for iris melanocyte pigmentation in early life, so a congenital lesion leaves the affected iris lighter (heterochromia iridis).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: How is a confirmed Horner's syndrome imaged once localised?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back:
By level:
  • MRI brain / cord (first-order)
  • CXR / CT chest apex (second-order / Pancoast)
  • CT / MR angiography of the neck (third-order / dissection)
  • urinary catecholamines + imaging in a child.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: Why can apraclonidine be falsely negative in a very acute Horner's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: Denervation supersensitivity takes ~1–2 weeks to develop, so apraclonidine may not yet reverse the anisocoria in the first few days — exactly the window of a painful dissection. Use cocaine to confirm acutely.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.front: In Horner's syndrome, which pupil is abnormal and is vision affected?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Horner's Syndrome.back: The small (miotic) pupil is the abnormal one (anisocoria worse in the dark) — contrast a CN III palsy / Adie’s where the large pupil is abnormal (worse in light). Horner’s does not reduce acuity or cause an RAPD.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What is nystagmus and how is jerk nystagmus named?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back:
An involuntary rhythmic oscillation of the eyes.
  • Jerk nystagmus has a slow drift and a fast corrective phase and is named by the direction of the fast phase
  • pendular nystagmus is equal-speed to-and-fro.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What features should you describe in any nystagmus?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back:
• Jerk vs pendular
  • the direction of the fast phase
  • the plane (horizontal / vertical / torsional)
  • whether it is in primary gaze or only gaze-evoked
  • whether it is conjugate or dissociated
  • and the effect of fixation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: How does visual fixation help separate peripheral from central nystagmus?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back:
• Peripheral (vestibular) nystagmus is suppressed by visual fixation (and worse behind Frenzel goggles)
  • central nystagmus is not suppressed and may even increase with fixation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What are the features of peripheral (vestibular) nystagmus?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back:
• Unidirectional (fast phase away from the lesion)
  • horizontal-torsional (never purely vertical)
  • suppressed by fixation
  • fatigable (positional / BPPV)
  • with prominent vertigo, nausea and often tinnitus / hearing loss.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What are the features of central nystagmus?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back:
• Direction-changing (fast phase follows gaze)
  • can be purely vertical or torsional
  • not suppressed (or worse) with fixation
  • usually less vertigo but with other brainstem / cerebellar signs.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What does downbeat nystagmus localise to?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: A craniocervical-junction lesion — classically an Arnold-Chiari malformation or foramen-magnum lesion; also cerebellar degeneration, lithium and Wernicke’s.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What does upbeat nystagmus suggest?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: A medullary or pontomesencephalic lesion (brainstem stroke, MS, tumour) or Wernicke’s encephalopathy — a central sign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What is internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF): failure of adduction of the ipsilateral eye on horizontal gaze with nystagmus of the abducting (contralateral) eye; convergence is preserved.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What causes an INO, and what does a bilateral INO in a young adult suggest?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back:
• Unilateral INO is usually a brainstem stroke
  • a bilateral INO, especially in a young adult, is multiple sclerosis until proven otherwise.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: Why is purely vertical nystagmus important?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: It is central until proven otherwise — peripheral vestibular lesions never produce a purely vertical nystagmus; it points to the brainstem or cerebellum.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What is the HINTS examination and what does it show in a stroke?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: Head-Impulse, Nystagmus, Test-of-Skew in acute continuous vertigo. A central (stroke) pattern is a normal head-impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus, or a skew deviation — more sensitive than early MRI.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: Which HINTS pattern is reassuring for a peripheral cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back:
• An abnormal (positive) head-impulse test (a corrective saccade)
  • unidirectional nystagmus and no skew
— consistent with a peripheral vestibular lesion (e.g. vestibular neuritis).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: Which drugs commonly cause nystagmus?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back:
• Phenytoin (and other anticonvulsants)
  • alcohol
  • and lithium (which can cause a persistent downbeat nystagmus)
— usually gaze-evoked.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What is the classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: Ophthalmoplegia / nystagmus, ataxia and confusion in an alcoholic or malnourished patient — give thiamine immediately (before glucose).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What is gaze-evoked nystagmus and what causes it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: Nystagmus that appears only on eccentric gaze, with the fast phase in the direction of gaze; a few beats at extremes is physiological (end-point), but sustained gaze-evoked nystagmus suggests cerebellar disease or drugs.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What is congenital nystagmus?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: A nystagmus present from early infancy, usually horizontal and pendular, that dampens on convergence and has a null point; vision is often relatively preserved and there is no oscillopsia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: Which investigations are used for a suspected central nystagmus?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: MRI of the brain (DWI for stroke) and the craniocervical junction (downbeat), ± MR angiography; consider drug levels and thiamine, and audiometry if a peripheral cause is possible.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What is oscillopsia and which nystagmus tends to cause it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: The illusion that the world is moving / bouncing; it is typical of acquired nystagmus (e.g. central or vestibular) and is characteristically absent in congenital nystagmus.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What are the features of the positional nystagmus of BPPV on the Dix-Hallpike test?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: After a short latency (a few seconds) a transient, up-beating and torsional (geotropic) nystagmus appears, lasting <30 s, and it fatigues on repetition — the signature of posterior-canal BPPV.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.front: What does the caloric-testing mnemonic COWS mean?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Nystagmus.back: Cold Opposite, Warm Same: cold water in one ear drives the fast phase of nystagmus to the opposite side, warm water to the same side.A reduced response (canal paresis) indicates a peripheral vestibular lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What is a fasciculation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: A brief, spontaneous twitch of a single motor unit — a visible flicker under the skin at rest that does not move the joint. It usually reflects lower-motor-neuron (LMN) irritability (anterior horn / axon), and is also generated at the neuromuscular junction by anticholinesterases and suxamethonium.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: How does a fasciculation differ from a fibrillation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: A fasciculation is visible to the naked eye (a whole motor unit); a fibrillation is a single muscle-fibre discharge seen only on EMG, not visible clinically.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What is the single most important thing to assess when you see fasciculations?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: The company they keep — is there weakness, wasting or UMN signs? Isolated fasciculations with a normal exam are usually benign; fasciculations with weakness and wasting suggest motor neurone disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What combination of signs with fasciculations suggests motor neurone disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Progressive painless weakness + wasting + fasciculations + mixed UMN and LMN signs, with no sensory loss and often bulbar involvement — refer urgently.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What is benign fasciculation syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Isolated fasciculations (often calf, eyelid or thumb) with normal power, bulk, tone and reflexes and a normal EMG; worse with fatigue, caffeine, stress and exercise. The commonest cause — reassure.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: Why must the tongue be examined at rest for fasciculations?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: A protruded tongue normally quivers and is easily mistaken for fasciculation. Examine it at rest lying in the floor of the mouth; true tongue fasciculations with wasting point to bulbar-onset MND.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: Which sensory finding helps separate MND from other causes of weakness and wasting?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: MND is a pure motor disorder — there is no sensory loss. Sensory signs point instead to a radiculopathy, peripheral neuropathy or cord lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: Which drugs and toxins can cause fasciculations?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back:
• Caffeine
  • salbutamol / β-agonists
  • anticholinesterases / organophosphates
  • and suxamethonium (a depolarising neuromuscular blocker)

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What acute poisoning causes fasciculations with a cholinergic crisis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Organophosphate (anticholinesterase) poisoning: fasciculations plus salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, miosis and bradycardia — treat with atropine (± pralidoxime).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: Which metabolic and endocrine disturbances cause fasciculations?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Thyrotoxicosis and low magnesium (and other electrolyte disturbances) — check TFTs and U&E / Ca / Mg.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: Name some lower-motor-neuron causes of pathological fasciculations other than MND.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back:
• Radiculopathy / nerve-root compression
  • cervical spondylotic amyotrophy
  • peripheral neuropathy
  • old polio / post-polio syndrome
  • spinal muscular atrophy
  • and syringomyelia

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What is the key investigation for fasciculations with suspected pathological cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: EMG / nerve conduction studies — showing denervation and reinnervation (widespread in MND); add TFTs, U&E / Ca / Mg, CK and MRI spine if focal.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What is post-polio syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: New weakness, wasting, fasciculations and fatigue appearing decades after acute poliomyelitis, in muscles previously affected — from failure of the overextended surviving motor units.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What is Isaac's syndrome (neuromyotonia)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Continuous muscle-fibre activity — fasciculations, cramps, stiffness and delayed relaxation — often autoimmune (anti-VGKC / CASPR2 antibodies); EMG shows myokymic / neuromyotonic discharges.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: How does myokymia differ from fasciculation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Myokymia is a continuous, undulating ‘bag-of-worms’ movement (e.g. facial myokymia in MS or a pontine lesion), whereas a fasciculation is a single brief twitch.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: How common are benign fasciculations in healthy people?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Very common — most healthy adults experience occasional fasciculations, especially of the eyelid or calf and after caffeine, exercise, stress or tiredness. With a normal exam they need no investigation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What features make fasciculations in a limb suggest a focal radiculopathy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Fasciculations and wasting confined to one myotome, with root (dermatomal) pain and a depressed reflex — investigate with MRI of the spine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: Which suxamethonium effect involves fasciculations?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Suxamethonium (a depolarising blocker) causes transient fasciculations at induction before paralysis, and is associated with post-operative myalgia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: Do neuromuscular-junction disorders (e.g. myasthenia gravis) or myopathies cause fasciculations?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: No — fasciculations are a marker of LMN / denervation. Pure NMJ disease (myasthenia) and most myopathies cause fatigable or proximal weakness without fasciculations.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: How is tetany distinguished from fasciculation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Tetany is sustained muscle spasm (carpopedal spasm, peri-oral tingling, positive Chvostek / Trousseau) from hypocalcaemia / hypomagnesaemia — not a brief single-motor-unit flicker.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.front: What is cramp-fasciculation syndrome and how does it relate to Isaac's syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Fasciculations.back: Cramps + fasciculations with a normal or near-normal EMG — the benign end of the peripheral-nerve-hyperexcitability spectrum, of which Isaac’s (neuromyotonia), with neuromyotonic discharges and anti-VGKC/CASPR2 antibodies, is the severe end.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: What is foot drop and how does it affect gait?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Weakness of ankle dorsiflexion (and toe extension) so the foot cannot be lifted; the toes catch, the foot slaps the floor, and the patient high-steps to clear it (a high-stepping / steppage gait).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: Which single bedside test best localises a foot drop, and why?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Inversion (tibialis posterior, L5 via the tibial nerve): it is spared in a common peroneal palsy (that nerve doesn’t supply it) but weak in an L5 radiculopathy — separating the two commonest causes.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: What is the commonest cause of an isolated foot drop?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: A common peroneal (fibular) nerve palsy from compression at the fibular neck — e.g. leg-crossing, prolonged squatting, a plaster cast, weight loss or local trauma.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: What is the motor and sensory pattern of a common peroneal nerve palsy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back:
• Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with inversion and the ankle jerk preserved
  • sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot and the lateral lower leg

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: What is the motor pattern of an L5 radiculopathy causing foot drop?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Weak dorsiflexion, inversion, eversion, toe extension AND hip abduction (a wider pattern than a peroneal palsy), with radicular (sciatica) pain and an L5 dermatomal sensory loss.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: How does the ankle jerk help localise a foot drop?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: It is an S1 reflex, so it is preserved in a peroneal palsy and in most L5 radiculopathies, but is lost when the lesion is at the sciatic nerve or the lumbosacral plexus / S1 root.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: Why does weak hip abduction point away from a peroneal nerve lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Hip abduction (gluteus medius) is supplied by L5 via the superior gluteal nerve, well proximal to the peroneal nerve. Its weakness means the L5 fibres are affected at the root or plexus, not at the fibular neck.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: What is the pattern of a sciatic nerve lesion causing foot drop?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Foot drop plus weak knee flexion (hamstrings) and weakness of all muscles below the knee, a lost ankle jerk, and sensory loss over most of the foot (sparing the medial saphenous territory).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: What features make a foot drop a red flag for cauda equina syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Bilateral foot drop with back pain, saddle anaesthesia and bladder / bowel disturbance — an emergency needing urgent MRI of the whole spine and decompression.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: Which features suggest a foot drop is due to a central / upper-motor-neuron lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Increased tone, brisk reflexes and an upgoing plantar (a spastic foot drop), ± a sensory level — from stroke, MS or cord disease, not a peripheral nerve.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: What is the key investigation to localise a peripheral foot drop?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Nerve conduction studies / EMG — a conduction block at the fibular neck confirms a peroneal palsy, whereas denervation in L5 muscles beyond the peroneal territory indicates a radiculopathy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: Which pattern of foot drop suggests Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: A bilateral, slowly progressive foot drop with pes cavus, distal (“inverted champagne bottle”) wasting, and often a family history — a hereditary sensorimotor neuropathy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: How can motor neurone disease cause foot drop?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: As an LMN pattern of weakness, wasting and fasciculations with no sensory loss, often with mixed UMN signs elsewhere — suspect it if a foot drop is progressive and painless with wasting.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: What is the typical management of a common peroneal palsy from external compression?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Avoid the compression (leg-crossing, tight casts), an ankle-foot orthosis (AFO) to hold the foot, and physiotherapy; most recover over weeks to months as the nerve remyelinates.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: What is mononeuritis multiplex and how might it present with foot drop?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: Several individual nerves affected sequentially (e.g. a peroneal palsy plus another nerve) — classically from diabetes or vasculitis; screen with glucose, ESR/CRP and an autoimmune / vasculitis panel.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: Why is a rapidly progressive bilateral foot drop with areflexia important?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: It suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome (ascending weakness, areflexia, albuminocytological dissociation on LP) — monitor respiratory function (FVC) as it can progress to respiratory failure.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: Which muscles perform ankle inversion and eversion, and what supplies them?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back:
• Inversion: tibialis posterior (tibial nerve, L5)
  • eversion: peroneus longus & brevis (superficial peroneal nerve, L5/S1)
Tibialis anterior also assists inversion but is deep-peroneal, so test inversion with the foot plantarflexed to isolate tibialis posterior. Eversion is weak in a peroneal palsy; inversion is not.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: How does functional electrical stimulation (FES) differ from an ankle-foot orthosis for foot drop?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: An AFO passively splints the ankle in dorsiflexion; FES stimulates the common peroneal nerve during swing phase to actively dorsiflex the foot. FES needs an intact peroneal nerve and muscle, so it suits UMN / central foot drop more than a denervating lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: How do deep and superficial peroneal nerve lesions differ?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back:
• Deep peroneal: weak dorsiflexion / toe extension with sensory loss in the first web space
  • Superficial peroneal: weak eversion with sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot
A common peroneal palsy affects both.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.front: How does gluteus medius (L5) weakness present, and why does it matter in foot drop?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Foot Drop.back: It causes a Trendelenburg sign / gait (pelvis drops on the swing side / a waddle). Weak hip abduction with a foot drop places the L5 lesion at the root or plexus — proximal to the peroneal nerve at the fibular neck.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: Resistance and pain on passive flexion of the neck (chin toward chest) in a relaxed patient — an elicited sign, most importantly of meningeal irritation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: How does meningeal neck stiffness differ from cervical-spine stiffness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back:
• Meningeal: resists flexion but rotates / laterally flexes relatively freely.
  • Cervical-spine: resists all movements.
Meningeal stiffness usually has fever / headache / photophobia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: Which two dangerous causes must neck stiffness always prompt?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: Meningitis (fever + headache + stiffness ± rash) and subarachnoid haemorrhage (thunderclap headache) — both need urgent action.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: What is the immediate action for fever, headache, neck stiffness and a non-blanching rash?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: Treat as meningococcal meningitis: parenteral benzylpenicillin / ceftriaxone immediately (in the community too), then transfer — do not wait for tests.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: How sensitive is neck stiffness for meningitis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: Imperfect — it can be absent in early, very young, elderly or immunosuppressed patients, so a supple neck does not exclude meningitis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: What is jolt accentuation and why is it useful?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: Headache that worsens when the patient rotates the head 2–3 times per second — a bedside sign of meningeal irritation. Its sensitivity is disputed, so a negative jolt does not exclude meningitis.

• Cervical spondylosis
  • muscle spasm
  • trauma / fracture
  • and rheumatoid atlantoaxial instability
— resistance in all directions, no meningism pattern.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: Why must neck stiffness after trauma be treated cautiously?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: It may reflect a cervical-spine injury / fracture — immobilise the neck and image before moving it.
Neck stiffness from a systemic infection (tonsillitis, pneumonia, UTI), classically in children who look well between episodes and have a normal CSF.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: Which local (extracranial) infections can cause neck stiffness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back:
• Retropharyngeal abscess
  • severe tonsillitis
  • and cervical lymphadenitis
— consider these especially in children.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: How does tetanus present differently from isolated neck stiffness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: With generalised rigidity — trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus and opisthotonos — rather than isolated resistance to neck flexion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: Which two signs are elicited alongside neck stiffness in the meningism screen?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back:
• Kernig’s sign (hip flexed → knee extension pain)
  • and Brudzinski’s sign (neck flexion → hip / knee flexion).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: In suspected bacterial meningitis, what must not be delayed by the LP?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: Antibiotics — take blood cultures and give antibiotics first; the LP follows once safe (CT first if reduced GCS, focal signs or papilloedema).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: When is a CT needed before LP in a patient with neck stiffness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: If there is reduced / fluctuating GCS, focal neurological signs, papilloedema, seizures or immunocompromise — to exclude a mass and avoid coning.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: How is subarachnoid haemorrhage confirmed when neck stiffness follows a thunderclap headache?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: CT head first (near 100% sensitive early); if negative, LP at ≥12 h for xanthochromia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: Can raised intracranial pressure cause neck stiffness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: Yes — tonsillar herniation can produce neck stiffness, and it may accompany a falling GCS; treat as a neurosurgical emergency.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: What does neck stiffness with photophobia and headache but no fever suggest?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: Still consider subarachnoid haemorrhage and viral meningitis — meningeal irritation is not always febrile; investigate rather than reassure.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.front: Which bedside features best separate a meningitic from a mechanical stiff neck?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neck Stiffness.back: Fever, headache, photophobia, rash, positive Kernig’s / Brudzinski’s and jolt accentuation favour meningeal irritation; pain in all neck movements without these favours a mechanical cause.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: With the patient supine, flex the hip to 90° (knee bent), then passively extend the knee. Pain and hamstring resistance that limit extension are a positive sign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: What does a positive Kernig's sign indicate?
Why is Kernig's sign positive in meningeal irritation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Extending the knee with the hip flexed stretches the inflamed lumbosacral nerve roots and meninges, provoking protective pain and hamstring spasm.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: How sensitive and specific is Kernig's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Specific but insensitive — useful when positive, but frequently absent in proven meningitis, so a negative sign does not exclude it.
No — it is insensitive and often absent, especially early or in the very young, elderly or immunosuppressed. Investigate on the whole picture.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: What are the causes of a false-positive Kernig's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Lumbar radiculopathy / sciatica and hamstring pathology can limit knee extension painfully without meningeal irritation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: How does Kernig's sign differ from Brudzinski's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back:
• Kernig’s works from the leg (hip flexed → extend the knee → pain).
  • Brudzinski’s works from the neck (flex the neck → hips / knees flex).
Both test meningeal irritation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: Which signs complete the meningism screen with Kernig's?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back:
• Neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity)
  • and Brudzinski’s sign
  • plus photophobia and jolt accentuation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: What is the immediate action if Kernig's is positive with fever, headache and a rash?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Treat as meningococcal meningitis — blood cultures then parenteral antibiotics immediately; do not wait for the LP.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: What does a positive Kernig's with a thunderclap headache suggest?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Subarachnoid haemorrhage — blood irritating the meninges; investigate with CT then LP for xanthochromia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: How is the underlying cause of a positive Kernig's confirmed?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Lumbar puncture for CSF (cells, protein, glucose, culture, PCR); CT first if reduced GCS, focal signs or papilloedema.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: Which more sensitive bedside sign complements Kernig's for meningeal irritation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Jolt accentuation of headache — traditionally taught as more sensitive than Kernig’s, Brudzinski’s or neck stiffness, though its sensitivity is disputed and a negative jolt does not exclude meningitis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: In whom is Kernig's sign especially unreliable?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: The very young, the elderly, the immunosuppressed and the obtunded — meningism signs are frequently absent.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: Why must you never delay antibiotics while eliciting meningeal signs?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Because bacterial meningitis is time-critical and the signs are insensitive — a normal exam does not exclude it; give antibiotics on suspicion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: Is Kernig's sign usually unilateral or bilateral in meningitis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Typically bilateral, because meningeal irritation is diffuse; a strictly unilateral positive with back / leg pain suggests a radiculopathy instead.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: What CSF picture would a positive Kernig's from bacterial meningitis show?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Neutrophils, high protein and low glucose (< half serum) — the classic bacterial pattern.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: Which eye symptom commonly accompanies the meningeal irritation Kernig's detects?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: Photophobia (discomfort in bright light) is a common companion of meningeal irritation, alongside headache, fever and neck stiffness.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.front: How can meningococcal septicaemia present with little meningism?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Kernig's Sign.back: With a non-blanching purpuric rash, fever and shock but minimal neck stiffness / Kernig's — septicaemia can dominate over meningitis, so treat on the rash and give antibiotics immediately.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: With the patient supine and relaxed, passively flex the neck (chin toward chest). Involuntary flexion of the hips and knees is a positive sign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: What does a positive Brudzinski's sign indicate?
Why is Brudzinski's sign positive in meningeal irritation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Neck flexion tugs on the inflamed meninges; the patient reflexively flexes the hips and knees to reduce the painful stretch.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: How sensitive and specific is Brudzinski's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Specific but insensitive — helpful when clearly positive, but often absent in proven meningitis, so a negative sign does not exclude it.
No — it is insensitive and frequently absent; never use it to rule meningitis out. Investigate and treat on suspicion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: How does Brudzinski's sign differ from Kernig's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back:
• Brudzinski’s works from the neck (flex neck → hips / knees flex).
  • Kernig’s works from the leg (hip flexed → extend knee → pain).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: Which signs complete the meningism screen with Brudzinski's?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back:
• Neck stiffness
  • and Kernig’s sign
  • plus photophobia and jolt accentuation of headache.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: What is the immediate action if Brudzinski's is positive with fever, headache and a rash?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Treat as meningococcal meningitis — blood cultures then parenteral antibiotics immediately.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: What does a positive Brudzinski's with a thunderclap headache suggest?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Subarachnoid haemorrhage — investigate with CT then LP for xanthochromia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: In which patients is Brudzinski's sign hard to interpret or unreliable?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back:
• The obtunded
  • the very young
  • the elderly
  • and those with cervical-spine disease
— and it is insensitive generally.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: Which more sensitive bedside sign complements Brudzinski's?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Jolt accentuation of headache — traditionally taught as more sensitive than Brudzinski’s, Kernig’s or neck stiffness, though its sensitivity is disputed and a negative jolt does not exclude meningitis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: How is the underlying cause of a positive Brudzinski's confirmed?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Lumbar puncture for CSF; CT head first if reduced GCS, focal signs or papilloedema, and always give antibiotics first if bacterial meningitis is suspected.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: Besides the classic neck sign, what are the named Brudzinski variants?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: The classic is the nape-of-the-neck sign (neck flexion → hip / knee flexion); variants include the contralateral-leg and symphyseal / cheek signs — all reflect meningeal irritation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: Which physiological principle underlies both Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Both minimise painful traction on inflamed meninges and nerve roots — the body resists or repositions to reduce the stretch.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: What CSF finding would confirm subarachnoid haemorrhage in a patient with a positive Brudzinski's?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Xanthochromia (and red cells that do not clear across bottles) on an LP taken ≥12 h after onset.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: Why can meningeal signs be absent in an infant with meningitis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Infants often show non-specific features (irritability, poor feeding, a bulging fontanelle) rather than classic Brudzinski’s / Kernig’s — a high index of suspicion is needed.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: Does a positive Brudzinski's sign localise the cause within the CNS?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: No — it only signals diffuse meningeal irritation; the cause (infection vs blood) is determined by the history, CT and CSF.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.front: What must always accompany the finding of a positive Brudzinski's in a septic patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brudzinski's Sign.back: Urgent treatment — blood cultures + antibiotics (± the meningitis screen) — not just documentation of the sign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What is 'increased tone' and how is it assessed?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Increased resistance to passive movement of a limb, felt by moving the joint (elbow, wrist, knee) with the patient relaxed — assessed at varying speeds and compared side to side.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What is the key difference between spasticity and rigidity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Spasticity is velocity-dependent (worse when moved quickly, clasp-knife); rigidity is velocity-independent (constant throughout the range, lead-pipe or cogwheel).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What are the features of spasticity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Velocity-dependent resistance with a clasp-knife catch-and-give, in a pyramidal distribution (arm flexors, leg extensors), with brisk reflexes, clonus and an upgoing plantar (a UMN sign).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What are the features of rigidity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Velocity-independent resistance present throughout the range — lead-pipe (constant) or cogwheel — from an extrapyramidal (basal-ganglia) lesion, with bradykinesia and tremor.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What is cogwheel rigidity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Lead-pipe rigidity with a superimposed tremor, felt as a ratchety give during passive movement (e.g. rolling the wrist) — classic in Parkinson’s disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What is the 'clasp-knife' phenomenon?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: In spasticity, initial resistance to passive movement that suddenly gives way as movement continues — velocity-dependent and a UMN feature.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: Which company distinguishes spasticity (UMN) from rigidity (extrapyramidal)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back:
• Spasticity: pyramidal weakness, brisk reflexes, clonus, upgoing plantar
  • Rigidity: bradykinesia, resting tremor, postural instability (parkinsonism).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What is the typical distribution of spasticity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: The antigravity muscles — arm flexors and leg extensors — the classic pyramidal pattern of a cortical / internal-capsule lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: Which conditions cause spasticity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Stroke, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord lesions and cerebral palsy — any upper-motor-neuron pathology.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: Which conditions cause rigidity?
