signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Parkinson’s disease and drug-induced parkinsonism (antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) — extrapyramidal causes.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What is gegenhalten (paratonia)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Involuntary resistance to passive movement that increases in proportion to the force applied (the patient seems to oppose you) — a frontal-lobe / diffuse cerebral sign, often in dementia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What is decerebrate versus decorticate posturing?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Decerebrate = extension of the arms and legs (lower brainstem); decorticate = flexion of the arms with leg extension (above the brainstem). Both signal severe brain injury / raised ICP; decerebrate is worse.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: Which emergency causes acute generalised rigidity with fever?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (dopamine antagonist): rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability and a raised CK — stop the drug and treat urgently; consider serotonin syndrome and malignant hyperthermia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: How does tetanus present with increased tone?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Generalised rigidity with painful spasms, trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus and opisthotonos — from tetanospasmin; a clinical diagnosis needing urgent treatment.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: What is myotonia and how does it differ from rigidity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Delayed muscle relaxation after contraction (e.g. slow release of a handshake or eyelids after tight closure) — a muscle-membrane disorder (e.g. myotonic dystrophy), not a tone abnormality of central origin.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: How can bilateral spastic legs with a sensory level be localised?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: To a spinal cord lesion — spasticity, brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars below a sensory level indicate cord compression / myelopathy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: Which investigations follow a UMN (spastic) pattern of increased tone?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: MRI of the brain and/or spinal cord to find the upper-motor-neuron lesion; the level of spasticity and the sensory findings guide where to image.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: Why does drug history matter when assessing rigidity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Because drug-induced parkinsonism (antipsychotics, metoclopramide) is a common, reversible cause of rigidity — a medication review can resolve it, unlike idiopathic Parkinson’s disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: Why can an acute upper-motor-neuron lesion show REDUCED tone rather than spasticity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back: Because acute stroke or cord transection causes a spinal-shock / acute UMN phase of flaccidity and areflexia lasting hours to weeks; spasticity, brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars develop later.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.front: How is neuroleptic malignant syndrome distinguished from serotonin syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Increased Tone (Spa.back:
• NMS: a dopamine antagonist, slower onset, lead-pipe rigidity and hyporeflexia
  • Serotonin syndrome: a serotonergic drug, rapid onset, clonus / hyperreflexia / myoclonus, dilated pupils and GI upset.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Reduced resistance to passive movement — a floppy limb that flops and offers little resistance when moved or dropped; most often a lower-motor-neuron sign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: What company points to a lower-motor-neuron cause of flaccidity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Wasting, fasciculations and reduced / absent reflexes (± sensory loss) — the LMN pattern, in contrast to the spasticity and brisk reflexes of an established UMN lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: Why can an acute UMN lesion cause flaccidity rather than spasticity?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: In the acute phase (spinal shock) after a stroke or cord transection the limb is flaccid and areflexic for hours to weeks, only later becoming spastic with brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: Which flaccid presentation is a medical emergency to recognise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia — Guillain-Barré syndrome; monitor the forced vital capacity (FVC) for respiratory failure.
It causes hypotonia with pendular reflexes and other cerebellar signs (ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor) — a less-remembered cause of reduced tone.

Motor neurone disease, poliomyelitis and spinal muscular atrophy — flaccid, wasted, fasciculating muscles with reduced reflexes (no sensory loss). In MND the reflexes may instead be preserved or brisk, because it is often a mixed UMN + LMN disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: What is the reflex finding in a flaccid LMN lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Reduced or absent reflexes (hyporeflexia / areflexia) — unlike the brisk reflexes of an established UMN lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: Which acute spinal presentation causes flaccid paralysis with a sensory level?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Acute spinal cord injury or compression in the spinal-shock phase — flaccid, areflexic limbs below a sensory level with painless retention; image the whole spine urgently.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: How is a floppy infant with central hypotonia distinguished from peripheral?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back:
• Central (encephalopathy, HIE, syndromes): preserved / brisk reflexes and a depressed conscious level
  • Peripheral (SMA, congenital myopathy / neuropathy): weakness with reduced / absent reflexes and an alert infant.
Albuminocytological dissociation — a raised CSF protein with a normal cell count — typically after the first week; nerve conduction studies show a demyelinating neuropathy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: Which neuromuscular-junction disorders can cause a floppy / weak patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Myasthenia gravis and Lambert-Eaton (fatigable weakness, tone often normal) and botulism (descending flaccid paralysis with bulbar and autonomic features).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: How does a myopathy typically present in terms of tone and reflexes?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Proximal flaccid weakness with a raised CK and relatively preserved reflexes until late — distinguishing it from a neuropathy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: What is the key investigation for a flaccid LMN pattern?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Nerve conduction studies / EMG to distinguish neuropathy, anterior-horn disease and myopathy; add MRI, LP or CK depending on the pattern.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: Why does acute flaccidity NOT exclude an upper-motor-neuron lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Because the spinal-shock phase of an acute UMN lesion is flaccid and areflexic — use the sensory level and the time course (later evolves to spasticity) to localise.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: What is the classic presentation of botulism?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: A descending flaccid paralysis starting with bulbar signs (diplopia, dysphagia, dysarthria) and dilated pupils, from canned / preserved food or infant honey — give antitoxin.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: How does flaccidity from a peripheral neuropathy usually present?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Distal, symmetrical flaccid weakness with reduced reflexes and glove-and-stocking sensory loss — e.g. diabetic or other length-dependent neuropathy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: What must be monitored in a patient with ascending flaccid weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: Respiratory function (FVC) and bulbar / swallow safety — Guillain-Barré can progress to respiratory failure needing ventilation; also watch for autonomic instability.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: Which single feature best separates cerebellar hypotonia from an LMN cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: The company: cerebellar hypotonia has pendular reflexes and other cerebellar signs (ataxia, nystagmus) with no wasting or fasciculations, unlike an LMN lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.front: How does the sensory pattern separate an acute cord lesion from cauda equina when the legs are flaccid?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced Tone (Flacc.back: A sensory level on the trunk points to the spinal cord; saddle (perianal) sensory loss with flaccid, areflexic legs and painless retention points to cauda equina (a root / LMN lesion).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: What do brisk reflexes, clonus and an extensor plantar together indicate?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: An upper-motor-neuron (UMN) lesion — they arise from loss of descending corticospinal inhibition of the spinal reflex arc, and travel with spasticity and pyramidal weakness.

• 0 = absent
  • 1 = present (with reinforcement)
  • 2 = normal
  • 3 = brisk
  • 4 = very brisk with clonus.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: What is clonus and when is it pathological?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: Rhythmic involuntary muscle contractions on sudden sustained stretch (e.g. sharp ankle dorsiflexion). More than ~5 sustained beats is pathological (UMN); a couple of unsustained beats can be normal.
Stroking the lateral sole produces dorsiflexion (up-going) of the great toe with fanning of the toes — a UMN (extensor plantar) sign; a down-going toe is the normal flexor response.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: Why does a UMN lesion cause brisk reflexes?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: The corticospinal tract normally inhibits the spinal reflex arc; a UMN lesion removes that inhibition, disinhibiting the arc so reflexes become brisk, clonus appears and the plantar goes up.
A reflex that can be elicited from a larger-than-normal area around the tendon (e.g. tapping the lower tibia elicits the knee jerk) — a sign of hyperreflexia.
Tapping one knee (or the adductor tendon) produces adduction of the opposite leg — a spread of the reflex indicating hyperreflexia / a UMN lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: Which accompanying signs confirm that brisk reflexes are part of a UMN pattern?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: Increased tone (spasticity) and pyramidal-pattern weakness (weak extensors in the arm, weak flexors in the leg) — the rest of the UMN syndrome.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: How do you localise a UMN lesion causing brisk reflexes?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back:
• Below a sensory level → spinal cord
  • unilateral with face / arm → contralateral hemisphere / brainstem
  • generalised → diffuse or bilateral disease.
The upper-limb equivalent of an extensor plantar: flicking the middle fingernail causes reflex flexion of the thumb and index finger — a sign of a UMN lesion (e.g. cervical myelopathy).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: Why are brisk reflexes with wasting and fasciculations important?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: This mixed UMN + LMN picture (with no sensory loss) is the fingerprint of motor neurone disease — brisk reflexes in a wasted, fasciculating limb should prompt urgent referral.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: Which causes produce the UMN reflex cluster?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back:
• Stroke
  • multiple sclerosis
  • spinal cord compression / myelopathy
  • cerebral palsy
  • and (mixed) motor neurone disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: When can brisk reflexes and a few beats of clonus be normal?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: In anxious or young patients — symmetrically brisk reflexes with a couple of unsustained clonus beats and downgoing plantars are non-specific / physiological.
It causes generally brisk reflexes (with a quick relaxation phase) — but the plantar stays downgoing; it is a systemic, not a UMN, cause.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: What is an inverted supinator jerk and what does it localise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: Tapping the supinator (brachioradialis) tendon gives finger flexion instead of elbow flexion — it localises a lesion to C5/6 (LMN at that level, UMN below).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: Why is the Babinski sign sometimes unreliable, and how do you improve it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: A ticklish or withdrawing foot can give a misleading response; use the least-noxious stimulus, stroke the lateral sole firmly once, and repeat — interpret only a clear, reproducible up-going toe.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: What is the danger pattern of new UMN reflex signs below a level?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: New brisk reflexes, clonus and upgoing plantars below a sensory level suggest spinal cord compression — an emergency needing urgent whole-spine MRI.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: What investigation follows a UMN reflex pattern once localised?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: MRI of the relevant level — brain (cortical / brainstem) or spine (cord); add EMG if motor neurone disease is suspected.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.front: How does serotonin syndrome present in terms of reflexes?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Brisk Reflexes, Clo.back: With hyperreflexia and clonus (often lower-limb predominant, inducible or spontaneous), plus hyperthermia, agitation, dilated pupils and autonomic instability on a serotonergic drug (SSRI/SNRI, tramadol) — contrast the rigidity and hyporeflexia of NMS.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: What do reduced or absent reflexes indicate?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back:
Interruption of the reflex arc — a lower-motor-neuron (LMN) sign; the lesion can be anywhere along the arc:
  • afferent nerve / dorsal root
  • efferent (anterior horn / root / nerve)
  • the neuromuscular junction
  • or the muscle.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: What must you do before recording a reflex as absent?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Reinforce it — the Jendrassik manoeuvre (clench the teeth or hook the flexed fingers and pull apart) for leg reflexes; only if it stays absent with reinforcement is it truly absent.

• 0 = absent
  • 1 = present only with reinforcement
  • 2 = normal (3 = brisk, 4 = clonus for the UMN end).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: Which reflex root values should you know for localisation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Ankle = S1, knee = L3/4, biceps & supinator = C5/6, triceps = C7 — a single lost reflex localises to that root.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: What does a single lost reflex with a matching deficit indicate?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: A radiculopathy at that root level — e.g. a lost ankle jerk with S1 signs, or a lost biceps jerk with C5/6 signs; image the spine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: What reflex pattern fits a peripheral neuropathy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Distal, symmetrical loss — the ankle jerks go first — with glove-and-stocking sensory loss (diabetes, alcohol, B12, drugs).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: Which emergency causes generalised areflexia with ascending weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Guillain-Barré syndrome — ascending flaccid weakness with generalised areflexia; monitor the vital capacity (FVC) for respiratory failure.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: What does 'absent ankle jerks with extensor plantars' signify?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back:
A combined (mixed UMN + LMN) lesion — classically
  • subacute combined degeneration (B12)
  • motor neurone disease
  • Friedreich’s ataxia
  • or dual pathology (neuropathy + cord / brain lesion).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: Which neuromuscular-junction disorder gives reflexes that RETURN after exercise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — reduced reflexes that facilitate (reappear or strengthen) after brief exercise; often paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: What is the 'hung-up' (slow-relaxing) ankle jerk and what causes it?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: A reflex with a normal contraction but a delayed relaxation phase (Woltman sign) — classically hypothyroidism.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: How do reduced reflexes differ from cerebellar pendular reflexes?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Cerebellar reflexes are pendular (the limb swings several times) rather than reduced / absent — a different sign reflecting hypotonia, not an interrupted arc.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: Which anterior-horn disease can show LMN areflexia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Motor neurone disease (LMN-predominant), spinal muscular atrophy and old polio — with wasting and fasciculations but no sensory loss.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: What CSF result supports Guillain-Barré as a cause of areflexia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Albuminocytological dissociation — raised protein with a normal cell count; nerve conduction studies show a demyelinating neuropathy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: Why can an acute upper-motor-neuron lesion give absent reflexes?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: In the spinal-shock phase after an acute cord (or brain) lesion, reflexes are transiently absent before becoming brisk — so acute areflexia does not exclude a UMN lesion.
A sensory neuropathy or a dorsal root / dorsal root ganglion lesion (e.g. tabes dorsalis) — breaking the sensory side of the arc removes the reflex.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: What is the first-line investigation for a reduced-reflex (LMN) pattern?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Nerve conduction studies / EMG to localise (neuropathy vs anterior horn vs NMJ vs muscle); add B12, glucose / HbA1c, TFTs and imaging as guided.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: Which benign syndrome combines absent tendon reflexes with a tonic pupil?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Holmes-Adie syndrome — a tonic (Adie’s) pupil (large, slow to react) with absent ankle / knee jerks, classically in a young woman; it is benign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: Why must plantars always be checked when a reflex is reduced?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: Because absent ankle jerks with an upgoing plantar reveal a combined UMN + LMN lesion (e.g. B12 / SACD, MND) — a pattern that changes the whole differential.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.front: What is the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Reduced / Absent Re.back: The triad of areflexia + ophthalmoplegia + ataxia (associated with anti-GQ1b antibodies) — a GBS variant to recognise when areflexia comes with eye-movement and gait signs.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back:
• Anosmia = complete loss of the sense of smell
  • hyposmia = a reduced sense of smell
It is the symptom of a lesion of the olfactory pathway (CN I) or of odorants being blocked from the olfactory epithelium.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: Why do patients with anosmia usually complain of losing their sense of taste?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: Because flavour is mostly smell (retronasal olfaction) — the tongue only detects the five basic tastes, so when smell goes, food tastes bland even though true taste is intact.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: How should the sense of smell be tested at the bedside?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: Test each nostril separately (occlude the other) with a non-irritant odour — e.g. coffee or vanilla; ask the patient to identify it. Avoid menthol / peppermint, which also stimulate the trigeminal nerve.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: Why must ammonia / smelling salts NOT be used to test smell?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: They are irritants that stimulate the trigeminal nerve (CN V), not the olfactory nerve — a patient with true anosmia will still sense them, giving a false result.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: What is the commonest category of anosmia, and is it reversible?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back:
Conductive (sinonasal) anosmia — odorants cannot reach the epithelium:
  • rhinosinusitis
  • nasal polyps
  • allergic rhinitis
  • a cold / URTI
It is common and usually reversible.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: List the main sensorineural causes of anosmia.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back:
• Post-viral (including COVID-19)
  • head trauma
  • ageing (presbyosmia)
  • and toxins / smoking
(Neurodegeneration and subfrontal tumours are usually classed separately as central causes.)
By shearing of the olfactory fila as they pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid — a deceleration / frontal injury tears the fine nerve filaments.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: What does anosmia with clear nasal fluid after head injury suggest?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: A cribriform-plate fracture with CSF rhinorrhoea — test the fluid for β-2-transferrin; it carries a meningitis risk and needs neurosurgical input.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: What does UNILATERAL anosmia suggest until proven otherwise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: A subfrontal mass — classically an olfactory groove meningioma or a frontal-lobe tumour compressing one olfactory tract; it warrants an MRI brain.
Ipsilateral optic atrophy + ipsilateral anosmia + contralateral papilloedema, caused by a subfrontal (olfactory groove) tumour — direct compression on one side, raised ICP on the other.
Anosmia + hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (delayed / absent puberty) — a failure of the GnRH neurons and olfactory neurons to migrate together in development.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: Why is new anosmia relevant to neurodegenerative disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: Anosmia is an early (premotor) feature of Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s, often appearing years before the motor or cognitive signs.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: What is post-viral olfactory loss and its course?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: Anosmia following a viral URTI (including COVID-19) — often an isolated, sudden loss that may partially recover over months; olfactory training can help.
The gradual, age-related decline in the sense of smell — a common cause of reduced smell in older adults with no nasal disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: What is the first-line investigation for unilateral or centrally-suggestive anosmia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: MRI brain (focused on the anterior cranial fossa / olfactory grooves) to exclude a subfrontal tumour.
The UPSIT (University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test) or “Sniffin’ Sticks” — standardised scratch-and-sniff / pen kits that grade the degree of loss.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: Why is anosmia a safety issue as well as a quality-of-life problem?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: Patients cannot smell gas leaks, smoke or spoiled food — a real hazard; they also lose much of the pleasure of eating, which can affect nutrition and mood.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.front: Which investigation confirms that post-traumatic nasal fluid is CSF?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Anosmia.back: β-2-transferrin (or β-trace protein) testing of the fluid — it is specific to CSF; high-resolution CT localises the skull-base defect.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back: Skin and eye signs of a neurocutaneous syndrome, in which the skin and nervous system (both ectodermal) are affected together, with hamartomas and a raised tumour risk. Most are inherited (usually autosomal dominant) — e.g. NF1, NF2, tuberous sclerosis — but Sturge-Weber is sporadic (a somatic GNAQ mutation).

• ≥6 café-au-lait macules
  • axillary / inguinal freckling (Crowe’s sign)
  • and cutaneous / plexiform neurofibromas
— plus Lisch nodules in the eye.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: What size / number of café-au-lait macules is significant in NF1?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back: Six or more, each >5 mm before puberty or >15 mm after puberty.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: What are Lisch nodules and which syndrome do they indicate?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back: Iris hamartomas (pigmented, seen on slit-lamp) — specific to NF1; they are harmless but a useful diagnostic sign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: What is the gene / inheritance of NF1?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back: NF1 gene on chromosome 17 encoding neurofibromin (a tumour suppressor); autosomal dominant.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: What is the hallmark of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back: Bilateral vestibular (acoustic) schwannomas → progressive sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance; few skin signs. Also meningiomas, ependymomas and juvenile cataract (gene merlin, chromosome 22).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: List the classic skin signs of tuberous sclerosis.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back:
• Ash-leaf macules (hypopigmented)
  • adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas)
  • shagreen patch (lumbar connective-tissue naevus)
  • and periungual / subungual fibromas (Koenen tumours)
A cluster of facial angiofibromas over the malar region in tuberous sclerosis — despite the name it is neither sebaceous nor an adenoma.
With a Wood’s (ultraviolet) lamp, which makes the hypopigmented macules stand out — often the earliest sign of tuberous sclerosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: What is the Vogt triad of tuberous sclerosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back: Epilepsy + learning disability + adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas) — though not all three are always present.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: Name the key systemic hamartomas of tuberous sclerosis.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back:
• Cortical tubers & subependymal nodules / SEGA (brain)
  • cardiac rhabdomyoma
  • renal angiomyolipoma
  • retinal astrocytic hamartoma
  • and pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis
Genes TSC1 (hamartin) / TSC2 (tuberin).

A facial port-wine stain in the trigeminal V1 (ophthalmic) distribution + an ipsilateral leptomeningeal angioma → seizures, hemiparesis, learning disability and glaucoma; “tram-track” gyriform calcification.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: Why must the eye be examined in Sturge-Weber syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back: Because of the risk of glaucoma on the side of the port-wine stain — it can cause visual loss and needs monitoring.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: What is a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST) and how does it present in NF1?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back: Malignant transformation of a (plexiform) neurofibroma — suspect it when a lesion becomes rapidly enlarging, painful or hard, or causes new neurological deficit.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: Which tumours / vascular lesions occur in NF1 besides neurofibromas?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back:
• Optic pathway glioma (visual loss in a child)
  • other CNS gliomas
  • phaeochromocytoma and renal artery stenosis (hypertension)
  • and bony dysplasia (sphenoid wing, pseudarthrosis)
An AD phakomatosis with retinal and cerebellar / spinal haemangioblastomas, phaeochromocytoma, clear-cell renal cell carcinoma and pancreatic cysts (gene VHL, chromosome 3); skin signs are minimal.

An autosomal recessive disorder (ATM gene) with
  • oculocutaneous telangiectasia (conjunctival)
  • progressive cerebellar ataxia
  • immunodeficiency
  • a raised AFP
  • and increased malignancy risk

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.front: What is the general work-up when neurocutaneous stigmata are found?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Neurocutaneous Stig.back:
• Apply the diagnostic criteria
  • examine skin (Wood’s lamp), eyes (slit-lamp), BP and hearing
  • arrange MRI brain ± spine, systemic imaging (renal / cardiac) and genetic testing / counselling with MDT surveillance

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: Proprioception (joint-position sense) — specifically whether a dorsal-column / sensory ataxia is being compensated for by vision. It is not a test of cerebellar function.
The patient stands with feet together and arms by the sides; you confirm they are steady with the eyes open, then ask them to close their eyes — standing close, ready to catch them.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: What counts as a POSITIVE Romberg's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: A marked increase in sway, or a fall, that appears only when the eyes are closed (a small amount of sway with eyes closed is normal).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: Explain the 'two-of-three' rule behind Romberg's sign.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back:
Steady standing needs at least two of three inputs:
  • vision
  • proprioception (dorsal columns)
  • and vestibular
If proprioception is lost, vision compensates; closing the eyes removes vision, leaving only vestibular → the patient falls.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: Why must the patient be steady with the eyes OPEN before the test?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: Because if they are already unsteady with the eyes open the problem is cerebellar (or vestibular), and Romberg’s cannot be interpreted — the sign specifically looks for deterioration on removing vision.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: A positive Romberg indicates which type of ataxia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: A sensory (proprioceptive / dorsal-column) ataxia — NOT a cerebellar ataxia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: Why is a positive Romberg NOT a cerebellar sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: A cerebellar patient is unsteady with the eyes open as well, so they never achieve the steady baseline the test needs; their instability does not appear only on eye closure.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: List the dorsal-column causes of a positive Romberg's sign.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back:
• Subacute combined degeneration (B12)
  • tabes dorsalis (neurosyphilis)
  • Friedreich’s ataxia
  • and MS plaques affecting the dorsal columns

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: Which peripheral cause commonly gives a positive Romberg?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: A large-fibre sensory peripheral neuropathy — most often diabetic, but also alcohol, B6 toxicity, and paraneoplastic / immune sensory neuronopathy.
A positive Romberg with absent ankle jerks AND upgoing plantars — a mixed dorsal-column + corticospinal picture; check B12 as it is reversible if treated early.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: What eye sign accompanies the sensory ataxia of tabes dorsalis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: Argyll Robertson pupils (small, irregular, accommodate but do not react to light) — with lightning pains and absent reflexes in tertiary neurosyphilis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: What gait goes with a positive Romberg (sensory ataxia)?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: A stamping, high-stepping gait in which the patient watches their feet and is worse in the dark or with eyes closed.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: Which bedside modalities should you test to confirm a sensory ataxia?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: Joint-position sense and vibration sense (start distally at the great toe), plus reflexes and plantars — large-fibre dorsal-column modalities are impaired.
Elaborate swaying from the hips without actually falling, often improving with distraction — inconsistent with a true proprioceptive deficit.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: What blood tests are key when a positive Romberg is found?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: B12 and folate, glucose / HbA1c and syphilis serology — the reversible / treatable causes; add U&E, TFTs and nerve conduction studies as guided.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: Which spinal tracts, when diseased, produce a positive Romberg?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: The dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis & cuneatus) carrying proprioception and vibration from the periphery to the medulla.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: In Friedreich's ataxia, why can signs seem 'mixed'?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: Because it damages both the dorsal columns / sensory nerves (positive Romberg, absent reflexes) and the corticospinal / cerebellar pathways (upgoing plantars, cerebellar ataxia) — with pes cavus and scoliosis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.front: What is the significance of a RAPIDLY progressive sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Romberg's Sign.back: Consider a paraneoplastic or immune sensory neuronopathy (e.g. anti-Hu) — investigate for an underlying malignancy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: Support the patient’s relaxed hand, steady the middle finger, then flick (nip) the nail / distal phalanx downward and let it flick back.
Reflex flexion and adduction of the thumb (often with flexion of the index / other fingers) in response to flicking the middle-finger nail.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: What type of sign is Hoffmann's, and what is its upper-limb analogue?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: An upper-motor-neuron (UMN) sign — a disinhibited finger-flexor reflex; it is the hand’s analogue of the Babinski (plantar) response.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: Where does a positive Hoffmann's sign localise the lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: To the corticospinal (pyramidal) tract rostral to C5/6 — i.e. the cervical cord or the brain.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: Why is Hoffmann's sign LESS specific than Babinski?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: Because it can be present in normal people — especially the young and generally hyper-reflexic — so a symmetric sign in isolation may be benign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: When does a positive Hoffmann's sign become clinically significant?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: When it is asymmetric or new, or accompanied by other UMN signs (spasticity, brisk reflexes, clonus, upgoing plantars).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: What is the commonest cause of a pathological Hoffmann's sign in older adults?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: Cervical spondylotic (degenerative) myelopathy — the commonest cause of cord dysfunction in older adults.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: Which clinical picture should prompt urgent imaging when Hoffmann's is positive?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: Clumsy hands + a spastic gait + urinary urgency (± a sensory level / Lhermitte’s) — cervical myelopathy; arrange an MRI cervical spine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: Which UMN signs typically accompany a pathological Hoffmann's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: Increased tone (spasticity), brisk (hyper-active) reflexes, clonus and upgoing plantars — sometimes an inverted supinator reflex.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: What is the Trömner variant of Hoffmann's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: Flicking the volar (palmar) surface of the fingertip upward instead of the nail — it tests the same disinhibited finger-flexor reflex.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: What is an 'inverted supinator reflex' and where does it localise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: When eliciting the supinator (brachioradialis) jerk there is no brachioradialis contraction but finger flexion instead — it localises a lesion at the C5/6 level.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: Besides cervical myelopathy, list causes of a positive Hoffmann's sign.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back:
• Cord compression (disc / tumour)
  • multiple sclerosis (cervical plaque)
  • stroke / brain lesions
  • and the UMN component of motor neurone disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: Why must both hands be tested for Hoffmann's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: Because the sign is most meaningful when asymmetric — a unilateral or clearly asymmetric response is far more likely to be pathological than a symmetric one.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: What is the first-line investigation for a pathological Hoffmann's sign with myelopathic features?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: MRI of the cervical spine (looking for cord compression and cord signal change); MRI brain and whole cord if MS or a higher lesion is suspected.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: What is the management principle once cervical spondylotic myelopathy is confirmed?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: Neurosurgical assessment for decompression — timely surgery can halt progression, so a new myelopathy should not be left to deteriorate.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: How does a positive Hoffmann's sign differ mechanistically from a normal finger-flexor response?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: It reflects loss of corticospinal inhibition, exaggerating the deep finger-flexor reflex so a light stretch of one finger triggers thumb / finger flexion — hyperreflexia in the hand.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: Can a positive Hoffmann's sign occur with a purely LOWER-motor-neuron lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: No — it is a UMN sign; a pure LMN lesion causes reduced / absent reflexes, not a disinhibited finger-flexor reflex.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.front: In motor neurone disease, what makes Hoffmann's sign useful?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoffmann's Sign.back: It demonstrates the UMN component — a positive Hoffmann’s alongside wasting and fasciculations (LMN) and no sensory loss supports mixed UMN + LMN disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: Functional (non-organic) leg weakness from organic leg weakness — it is a bedside test for functional neurological disorder (FND).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: On what physiological principle does Hoover's sign rely?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: Crossed-extensor synergy — when one hip is flexed against resistance, the opposite hip extends automatically (involuntarily).

Patient supine: test hip extension of the weak leg directly (press the heel down — feels weak); then, with your hand under the weak heel, ask them to flex the GOOD hip against resistance and feel for downward pressure of the weak heel.

The weak leg’s hip extension is weak on direct (voluntary) testing but returns to normal (the heel presses down) when the opposite hip is flexed against resistance — i.e. weak voluntarily, normal automatically.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: Why is Hoover's a 'rule-in' sign rather than a diagnosis of exclusion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: Because it demonstrates a positive internal inconsistency (voluntary weakness with intact automatic movement) — positive evidence for functional weakness, not merely the absence of organic signs.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: Does a positive Hoover's sign mean the patient is faking?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: No. Functional weakness (FND) is genuine and involuntary; the sign shows the motor pathways are intact, not that the patient is deliberately withholding effort — it is not malingering.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: Can functional neurological disorder coexist with organic disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: Yes — FND can coexist with organic disease, so a positive Hoover’s does not by itself exclude a stroke or cord lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: Which red flags mean you must image despite a positive Hoover's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: A sensory level, bladder / bowel dysfunction, UMN signs (brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars) or a hyperacute onset — these mandate imaging regardless.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: Name other positive signs of functional weakness.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back:
• Give-way (collapsing) weakness
  • co-contraction of agonist and antagonist
  • drift without pronation
  • a dragging monoplegic gait
  • and midline splitting of sensation / vibration
In functional arm weakness the outstretched arm drifts downward without pronating — unlike an organic pyramidal drift, which pronates as it falls.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: Why is midline splitting of sensation a functional sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: Because organic sensory loss usually spares a 1–2 cm strip across the midline (dermatomal overlap), whereas exact midline splitting is non-physiological.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: Why is splitting of vibration sense over the sternum or forehead non-physiological?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: Because a single bone vibrates as one unit, so a reported difference between the two halves of the sternum / frontal bone cannot be organic.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: What is the dragging monoplegic gait of functional weakness?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: The weak leg is dragged behind as a dead weight (hip internally or externally rotated) rather than circumducted as in an organic hemiplegic gait.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: How should the diagnosis of FND be communicated to the patient?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: Transparently and without blame — explain (and ideally demonstrate Hoover’s) that it is a genuine, potentially reversible problem of nervous-system functioning, not damage or feigning.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: What is the management of functional neurological disorder?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back:
A positive explanation plus multidisciplinary rehabilitation —
  • physiotherapy and CBT
  • treat comorbid depression / anxiety
  • and avoid unnecessary investigations

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: Give two situations in which Hoover's sign cannot be reliably interpreted.
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back:
• When pain limits the effort
  • when there is genuine organic weakness of the contralateral hip flexors
  • or with inattention / neglect or bilateral leg weakness

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: Which muscle action is being tested (directly and indirectly) in Hoover's sign?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: Hip extension — tested directly (voluntary) in the weak leg, and indirectly / automatically as the synergist recruited during contralateral hip flexion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.front: What is functional neurological disorder (FND) formerly known as?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Hoover's Sign (Func.back: Conversion disorder (and it overlaps with ‘medically unexplained’ / somatoform presentations) — now understood as a genuine disorder of nervous-system function, diagnosed on positive signs.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 31-year-old woman has horizontal double vision. On left gaze her right eye fails to adduct past the midline, while the left eye abducts fully and shows jerk nystagmus. A lesion of which structure best explains this?
options: The left MLF, rostral to the left abducens nucleus
The right abducens (CN VI) nerve in the subarachnoid space
The right paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF)
The medial-rectus subnucleus of the right oculomotor (CN III) nerve
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: An INO is ipsilateral to the MLF lesion, so right-sided adduction failure means a right MLF lesion, not a left one. A CN VI nerve lesion causes abduction failure, and a PPRF lesion causes an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy in which neither eye crosses the midline.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A patient with a right INO is asked to look to the left. What is seen?
options: Failure of adduction of the right eye, with nystagmus of the abducting left eye
Failure of adduction of the left eye, with nystagmus of the abducting right eye
Failure of abduction of the right eye, with nystagmus of the adducting left eye
Failure of both eyes to cross the midline on left gaze, a complete horizontal gaze palsy
Failure of adduction of the right eye on left gaze and on near fixation, without nystagmus
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: Failure of adduction of the right eye, with nystagmus of the abducting left eye
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: INO is named for the side of the adduction failure. The last option is the pattern of a medial-rectus or third-nerve lesion, in which adduction also fails on near fixation and there is no dissociated nystagmus.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 29-year-old man has double vision; his right eye does not cross the midline on left gaze. Which single bedside finding would favour an internuclear (MLF) lesion over a partial right third-nerve palsy?
options: Adduction of the right eye is normal on near fixation
The right pupil is larger than the left and reacts sluggishly to light
There is a partial right ptosis that worsens after sustained upgaze
Upgaze and downgaze in the right eye are reduced as well as adduction
The right eye fails to adduct on near fixation as well as on left gaze
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: Adduction of the right eye is normal on near fixation
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: In INO the medial rectus and CN III are intact, so the eye still adducts on near fixation even though conjugate lateral gaze fails — convergence drives the medial recti through a separate supranuclear pathway that does not run in the MLF. A pupil-involving or vertically restricted pattern, or failure of adduction on near fixation too, points to CN III; a ptosis that worsens on sustained upgaze suggests myasthenia.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 27-year-old woman has bilateral INO. Two years ago she had painful visual loss in one eye that recovered over several weeks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: Bilateral demyelination of both MLFs with a previous episode of optic neuritis gives dissemination in time and space. Bilateral small-vessel infarction would be very unusual at this age, and neither myasthenia nor a glioma fits a remitting episode of painful monocular visual loss.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 74-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation notices double vision that came on over seconds while watching television. He has a unilateral INO and no other findings. What is the most likely cause?
options: A first demyelinating event of multiple sclerosis
Cavernous sinus thrombosis with an early third-nerve palsy
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: Abrupt onset in a vasculopath with atrial fibrillation fits a small-vessel infarct of the MLF; a demyelinating INO is more often subacute. Vestibular neuritis gives a unidirectional nystagmus with vertigo but no adduction failure, and cavernous sinus disease causes a painful ophthalmoplegia with proptosis and pupil involvement.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 35-year-old woman is found to have a new right INO. Which symptom is she most likely to report?
options: Horizontal double vision on left gaze, with oscillopsia
Loss of central vision in the right eye with red desaturation and pain on eye movement
A curtain descending over the left half of the visual field
Vertical double vision that is worst on reading down and in
Constant blurring of vision in both eyes, identical in every direction of gaze
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: Horizontal double vision on left gaze, with oscillopsia
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: The images separate horizontally on gaze away from the lesion, and the nystagmus of the other eye is often felt as oscillopsia. Many patients with INO have no symptoms at all, because the eyes are aligned in primary gaze. The second option describes optic neuritis, the third a homonymous field defect, and the fourth a fourth-nerve palsy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 68-year-old man develops diplopia abruptly. Neither eye will move to the right at all; on left gaze his right eye stops at the midline while his left eye abducts fully with nystagmus. Which syndrome does this describe?
options: An isolated paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF) gaze palsy
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: An MLF lesion together with the adjacent abducens nucleus or PPRF on the same side leaves abduction of the contralateral eye as the only remaining horizontal movement. An isolated PPRF lesion would give the gaze palsy without the adduction failure.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 44-year-old man has a large midline lesion of the upper brainstem. Neither eye will cross the midline on lateral gaze in either direction, and at rest both eyes are divergent. Which term describes this picture?
options: Bilateral sixth-nerve palsies from raised intracranial pressure
Duane retraction syndrome with globe retraction on adduction
Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia with ptosis
Parinaud's dorsal midbrain syndrome with light-near dissociation
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: WEBINO is a bilateral INO in which the eyes are divergent in the primary position, from a midline midbrain lesion involving both MLFs and the CN III medial-rectus subnuclei. Bilateral sixth-nerve palsies give failure of abduction, not adduction; CPEO is slowly progressive with ptosis; Parinaud's affects vertical gaze and the pupil reactions.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 58-year-old man develops sudden horizontal diplopia and is found to have a right INO with no other neurological signs. Which single investigation will best establish the cause?
options: MRI of the brain including the brainstem
MRI of the orbits focused on the extraocular muscles
Non-contrast CT head in the first hour after onset
Carotid Doppler ultrasound of both internal carotid arteries
Anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies with repetitive nerve stimulation
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: MRI of the brain including the brainstem
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: MRI is far more sensitive than CT for the small lesion responsible and separates a demyelinating plaque from an infarct — though a normal early scan does not exclude a small brainstem infarct, so repeat it if the picture fits. Orbital imaging looks at the muscles rather than the pathway, carotid studies assess the wrong circulation, and antibody testing addresses a mimic.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 26-year-old woman with a bilateral INO and a past episode of painful monocular visual loss is being investigated for multiple sclerosis. Which set of investigations is most appropriate?
options: MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast, lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands, and visual evoked potentials
Carotid Doppler, transthoracic echocardiogram, 24-hour ambulatory ECG and a vasculitis screen
Serum oligoclonal bands, plain skull radiographs and an electroencephalogram
CT of the chest for a thymoma, serum anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies, and repetitive nerve stimulation studies
Dix-Hallpike testing, pure-tone audiometry and MRI of the internal auditory meatus
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast, lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands, and visual evoked potentials
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: MRI with contrast and CSF oligoclonal bands establish dissemination in time and space; visual evoked potentials are a selective adjunct where the picture is equivocal, and MS is never diagnosed on MRI alone. Oligoclonal bands are a CSF test, not a serum one; the vascular and neuromuscular panels investigate a stroke and a mimic respectively; and the vestibular battery addresses a different presentation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 71-year-old man develops an INO abruptly. Which additional finding most strongly indicates that the lesion extends beyond the MLF into the basilar artery territory?
options: A vertical-gaze palsy with drowsiness and quadriparesis
A tender, pulseless temporal artery with jaw claudication
Severe neck pain with an ipsilateral partial Horner's syndrome
Bilateral leg weakness with a sensory level at T6
Limb numbness and urinary urgency that resolved over some weeks
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: A vertical-gaze palsy with drowsiness and quadriparesis
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: Additional brainstem signs — a vertical gaze problem, reduced consciousness or quadriparesis — place the lesion in the basilar territory and demand urgent imaging. The other options are all serious, but they localise to the temporal arteries, the carotid artery, the spinal cord and previous demyelination.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 30-year-old woman with known relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis develops a new INO over five days. MRI shows a new enhancing brainstem plaque. What is the most appropriate initial management?
options: A five-day course of oral methylprednisolone for the relapse
Intravenous immunoglobulin followed by plasma exchange
Intravenous thiamine, then glucose, for possible Wernicke's
Pyridostigmine with a trial of prednisolone for ocular myasthenia
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: A five-day course of oral methylprednisolone for the relapse
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: A subacute INO with an enhancing plaque in known MS is a relapse: once infection is excluded, treat with oral methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 5 days (intravenous if oral fails, is not tolerated, or admission is needed) and review disease-modifying therapy. Steroids hasten recovery but do not change the long-term outcome. Thrombolysis applies to hyperacute infarction, and the other options treat different diseases.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 52-year-old man with alcohol dependence and recent weight loss is admitted confused, with an INO, gait ataxia and nystagmus. What is the immediate priority?
options: Parenteral thiamine, given before any glucose
A CT head, then intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone
Thrombolysis for a presumed pontine infarct
Intravenous immunoglobulin for a suspected Miller Fisher variant
Intravenous glucose to clear the confusion, then oral vitamins
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: Parenteral thiamine, given before any glucose
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion in a malnourished patient is treated as Wernicke's encephalopathy and given high-dose parenteral thiamine empirically; glucose before thiamine can precipitate deterioration, and oral thiamine is not adequate. The usual eye signs are nystagmus and abduction weakness, with INO less common. Miller Fisher syndrome also pairs ophthalmoplegia with ataxia but is areflexic and subacute.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: A 38-year-old woman has intermittent horizontal diplopia. She appears to have a left INO, but after two minutes of sustained lateral gaze both a mild ptosis and the adduction deficit are clearly worse. Her pupils are normal. Which diagnosis must be excluded?
options: A partial left third-nerve palsy sparing the pupil
A demyelinating plaque of the left MLF
Thyroid eye disease restricting the medial rectus
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: Myasthenia can mimic an INO exactly; worsening with sustained effort, a variable deficit and normal pupils are the clues. Confirm with anti-acetylcholine-receptor antibodies and repetitive nerve stimulation. A true MLF plaque does not fatigue, and chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia is progressive rather than intermittent.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: You suspect a subtle right INO, but adduction looks almost normal when the patient follows your finger slowly. Which bedside manoeuvre is most likely to reveal the deficit?
options: Ask for rapid refixations between two widely spaced targets
Ask the patient to fixate a target brought slowly towards the nose
Hold eccentric gaze for thirty seconds and watch for drift back
Occlude each eye in turn and re-measure the deviation
Test optokinetic nystagmus with a rotating striped drum
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: Ask for rapid refixations between two widely spaced targets
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: A subtle INO can look near-normal on smooth pursuit; fast horizontal saccades between widely separated targets expose the slowing of the adducting eye relative to the abducting eye. Near fixation, gaze-holding, cover testing and optokinetic testing are all real bedside tests but assess other functions.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.question: An MRI is requested for an isolated INO. In which region should the radiologist look most carefully for the causative lesion?
options: The paramedian dorsal pons and midbrain tegmentum
The ventral pons at the level of the corticospinal tracts
The lateral medulla in the territory of PICA
The cavernous sinus and superior orbital fissure
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.answer: The paramedian dorsal pons and midbrain tegmentum
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Internuclear Ophtha.explanation: The tract responsible runs paramedian in the dorsal brainstem, and plaques or small infarcts there produce an INO. Ventral pontine, lateral medullary, cerebellar and cavernous sinus lesions each cause quite different eye-movement syndromes.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A 45-year-old describes a sudden 'worst headache of my life' that peaked in seconds. What is the first investigation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: A thunderclap headache is subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise — the first test is an urgent CT head.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A patient with a thunderclap headache has a normal CT head at 8 hours. What is the next step to exclude SAH?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: If CT is negative, do an LP at ≥12 h after onset to look for xanthochromia; a normal early CT does not fully exclude SAH.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A 72-year-old has a new temporal headache, scalp tenderness and jaw claudication. What is the immediate management?
options: Arrange routine ESR and review in 2 weeks
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: This is giant cell arteritis — give high-dose steroids immediately to prevent blindness; do ESR/CRP and biopsy, but do not delay steroids.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A patient has recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches lasting a day with nausea and photophobia, relieved by lying in a dark room. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: Unilateral throbbing headache, 4–72 h, with nausea and photophobia is migraine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A man has bouts of severe unilateral orbital pain with a watering red eye and a runny nose, lasting about an hour and waking him at night. What is the acute treatment?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: This is cluster headache; acute treatment is high-flow oxygen + SC sumatriptan.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A patient has a bilateral, band-like, pressing headache of moderate severity with no nausea and no worsening on activity. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: Bilateral, band-like, non-aggravated headache without nausea is a tension-type headache.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A patient has a headache that is worse on waking and on coughing, with morning vomiting and papilloedema. What is the priority investigation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: These features suggest raised intracranial pressure / a space-occupying lesion — image the brain (CT / MRI); LP before imaging is dangerous if there is a mass.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A patient has headache, fever, neck stiffness and photophobia. What is the most important immediate action?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: This is meningitis / encephalitis — give empirical antibiotics (± aciclovir) urgently; LP after CT if focal signs / reduced GCS.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A 30-year-old woman on the combined pill develops a persistent headache with seizures and a focal deficit. What is the likely diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: Headache with seizures / focal signs in a prothrombotic state (COCP) suggests cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — confirm with CT/MR venography.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A young obese woman has headache, papilloedema and transient visual obscurations, with normal brain imaging. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: Raised ICP with papilloedema and a normal scan in a young obese woman is idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A patient has paroxysmal, electric-shock-like pains in the cheek triggered by chewing and touch. What is the first-line treatment?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: This is trigeminal neuralgia; first-line treatment is carbamazepine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A patient with frequent migraines uses codeine or triptans on most days and now has a daily headache. What is the likely cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: Daily headache with frequent acute-medication use is medication-overuse headache — managed by withdrawing the overused drug.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A patient has a severe headache with a red painful eye, blurred vision with haloes, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and vomiting. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: Headache with a red painful eye, haloes, a fixed mid-dilated pupil and vomiting is acute angle-closure glaucoma — an ophthalmic emergency.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: A family all develop headaches and nausea that are worse at home in winter and improve when they go out. What is the likely cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: Headache affecting several household members, worse at home and in winter, suggests carbon monoxide poisoning — check carboxyhaemoglobin, give high-flow oxygen.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.question: Which of the following is a red-flag feature requiring urgent investigation of a headache?
options: Bilateral pressing pain relieved by rest
A long history of identical headaches
New headache over 50 with jaw claudication
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Headache.explanation: A new headache over 50 with jaw claudication (GCA) is a red flag; the others describe primary headaches without alarm features.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: A patient feels light-headed and 'about to black out' when standing, with no spinning sensation. How is this best classified?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Light-headedness / near-faint without an illusion of movement is presyncope (cardiovascular), not vertigo.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: A patient has brief episodes of spinning triggered by rolling over in bed, each lasting under a minute. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Brief, positional vertigo lasting seconds is BPPV — confirm with Dix-Hallpike and treat with the Epley manoeuvre.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: A patient has severe continuous vertigo for 3 days after a viral illness, with no hearing loss. What is the likely diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Acute prolonged vertigo with no hearing loss, often post-viral, is vestibular neuritis (labyrinthitis if hearing is affected).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: A patient has recurrent attacks of vertigo lasting hours with fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Episodic vertigo with fluctuating SNHL, tinnitus and aural fullness is Ménière's disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: In a patient with acute continuous vertigo, which HINTS finding suggests a central (stroke) cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: A NORMAL head impulse test in acute continuous vertigo is worrying for a central cause; an abnormal (catch-up saccade) head impulse is reassuringly peripheral.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: A patient with acute vertigo has vertical nystagmus, a skew deviation and cannot stand unaided. What is the priority?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Vertical nystagmus, skew and truncal ataxia are central signs — investigate for a posterior circulation stroke with MRI.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: A patient has gradual unilateral hearing loss and tinnitus with mild imbalance. Which investigation is most appropriate?
options: MRI of the internal acoustic meatus
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Progressive unilateral SNHL + tinnitus suggests an acoustic neuroma — image with MRI of the internal acoustic meatus.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: A young woman has recurrent vertigo with headache, photophobia and a history of migraine. What is the likely diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Vertigo with migrainous features and a migraine history is vestibular migraine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: An elderly patient on antihypertensives feels dizzy on standing. What bedside test confirms the cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Dizziness on standing suggests orthostatic hypotension — confirm with a lying-standing blood pressure.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: Which nystagmus feature indicates a central rather than peripheral cause of vertigo?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Vertical or direction-changing nystagmus is central; peripheral nystagmus is unidirectional, horizontal, fatigable and suppressed by fixation.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: What is the definitive treatment for BPPV?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: BPPV is treated with the Epley manoeuvre (canalith repositioning); vestibular sedatives are unhelpful.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: Why should prochlorperazine be limited to a few days in acute peripheral vertigo?
options: It worsens the head impulse test
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Prolonged vestibular sedatives impair central compensation and prolong symptoms — use only for a few days in acute severe vertigo.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: Which is a recognised preventive treatment for Ménière's disease?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Betahistine, salt restriction (± diuretics) are used to prevent Ménière's attacks; Epley is for BPPV.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: In which situation is the HINTS examination valid for separating peripheral from central vertigo?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: HINTS is only valid in active acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus); it is misleading in episodic, positional or resolved vertigo.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.question: A patient has acute vertigo with sudden occipital headache and neck pain. Which diagnosis must be considered?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo.explanation: Acute vertigo with sudden headache / neck pain raises vertebral artery dissection (a cause of posterior circulation stroke).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has increased tone, brisk reflexes and an upgoing plantar in the weak limb. Where is the lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Increased tone, hyperreflexia and an upgoing plantar are upper motor neuron signs.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient develops sudden right-sided face and arm weakness with brisk reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Acute focal UMN weakness is a stroke until proven otherwise — activate the stroke pathway.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has bilateral leg weakness, a sensory level at T10 and urinary retention. What is the priority?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: A sensory level with bilateral leg weakness and bladder involvement is cord compression — an emergency needing urgent MRI spine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has ascending flaccid weakness with absent reflexes 2 weeks after diarrhoea. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Ascending flaccid weakness with areflexia after an infection is Guillain-Barré syndrome; monitor FVC.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has fatigable weakness with drooping eyelids and double vision that worsen through the day. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Fatigable weakness with ptosis and diplopia is myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR antibodies).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has wasting and fasciculations in the hands with brisk reflexes and no sensory loss. What is the likely diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Mixed UMN (brisk reflexes) and LMN (wasting, fasciculations) signs with no sensory loss suggest motor neurone disease.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has proximal symmetrical weakness (struggling to stand from a chair), normal reflexes, no sensory loss and a raised CK. What is the likely diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Proximal symmetrical weakness with a raised CK and no sensory loss indicates a myopathy (e.g. myositis).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has distal symmetrical weakness and 'glove and stocking' sensory loss. Where is the lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Distal symmetrical weakness with glove-and-stocking sensory loss is a peripheral (poly)neuropathy.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has proximal weakness that improves after repeated effort, with a history of smoking. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Weakness that improves with use in a smoker is Lambert-Eaton syndrome (paraneoplastic, small-cell lung cancer).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has absent ankle jerks but upgoing plantars, with sensory ataxia. What is the likely diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Absent ankle jerks with extensor (upgoing) plantars is a classic mixed picture — think subacute combined degeneration of the cord (B12 deficiency); also MND, Friedreich's and taboparesis.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: Which investigation supports a diagnosis of Guillain-Barré syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: GBS shows albuminocytological dissociation (raised CSF protein, normal cell count) on lumbar puncture, with supportive nerve conduction studies.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: Which antibody is most associated with myasthenia gravis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Anti-acetylcholine-receptor (anti-AChR) antibodies are the classic association (anti-MuSK in some seronegative cases).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: Fasciculations in a wasted muscle indicate a lesion at which level?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Fasciculations (with wasting and reduced reflexes) are a lower motor neuron sign.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has back pain, flaccid weak legs, saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Flaccid (LMN) legs with saddle anaesthesia and urinary retention is cauda equina syndrome — an emergency needing urgent MRI (cord compression instead gives UMN legs + a sensory level).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.question: A patient has weakness in the muscles of one myotome with dermatomal sensory loss and shooting pain down the limb. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness.explanation: Myotomal weakness with dermatomal sensory loss and radicular pain indicates a radiculopathy (nerve-root lesion).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A diabetic patient has numbness affecting both feet in a symmetrical pattern up to the ankles. What is this pattern called?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Distal symmetrical loss is a glove-and-stocking polyneuropathy (length-dependent) — classically diabetic.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient has lost pain and temperature sensation but retained vibration and proprioception. Where does this dissociated loss localise?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Dissociated sensory loss (one modality set lost, the other spared) localises to the spinal cord.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient has ipsilateral leg weakness and vibration loss with contralateral loss of pain and temperature below a spinal level. What is the syndrome?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Ipsilateral dorsal-column + UMN signs with contralateral spinothalamic loss is Brown-Séquard (hemicord) syndrome.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A young patient has loss of pain and temperature over both shoulders and arms in a 'cape' distribution, with preserved light touch and vibration. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: A 'cape' distribution of dissociated pain / temperature loss with spared dorsal columns is syringomyelia (central-cord lesion).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient has loss of vibration and proprioception with upgoing plantars but absent ankle jerks. What is the likely cause?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Dorsal-column loss with upgoing plantars and absent ankle jerks suggests subacute combined degeneration (B12 deficiency).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient has sensory loss below the umbilicus with leg weakness and urinary symptoms. What is the priority investigation?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: A sensory level with weakness and bladder involvement indicates cord compression — the priority is urgent MRI spine.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient has complete loss of all sensory modalities down one side of the body after a stroke. Where is the lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Contralateral hemisensory loss of all modalities is classic of a thalamic lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient has numbness of the left side of the face and the right side of the body. Where is the lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Crossed sensory loss (ipsilateral face, contralateral body) localises to the brainstem (e.g. lateral medullary syndrome).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient can feel touch and pinprick normally but cannot identify objects placed in the hand or numbers drawn on the palm, and ignores stimuli on one side. Where is the lesion?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Impaired stereognosis, graphaesthesia and sensory inattention with preserved primary modalities indicate a parietal cortex lesion.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient has sensory loss over the lateral forearm and thumb with shooting pain down the arm. What is this pattern?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Dermatomal loss with radicular pain is a radiculopathy (nerve-root lesion).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient has tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers, worse at night, reproduced by tapping the wrist. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Median-nerve paraesthesia worse at night with a positive Tinel's sign is carpal tunnel syndrome.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: Which modalities are carried by the dorsal columns?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: The dorsal columns carry vibration, proprioception and fine touch; pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic tract.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A sensory level is found at the umbilicus. Which dermatome does this correspond to?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: The umbilicus is T10 (other anchors: nipple T4, groin L1, thumb C6, little finger C8, big toe L5) — useful for pinpointing a sensory level.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: A patient has saddle anaesthesia, flaccid weak legs and urinary retention. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: Saddle anaesthesia with flaccid legs and retention is cauda equina syndrome — an emergency needing urgent MRI.

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.question: Which investigations are most appropriate for a symmetrical glove-and-stocking sensory neuropathy?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Sensory Disturbance.explanation: A polyneuropathy is investigated with nerve conduction studies and a cause screen (glucose / HbA1c, B12, TFTs, U&E).

signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.question: An older patient has an asymmetric slow tremor of one hand that is present at rest and eases when reaching for a cup, with bradykinesia. What is the diagnosis?
signs__NEUROLOGICAL__Tremor.explanation: An asymmetric rest tremor that eases on movement, with bradykinesia and rigidity, is Parkinson’s disease.
